title: ENTERPRISE AGENTIC AI FOR AUTONOMOUS SOURCING: DESIGNING A SECURE MULTI-AGENT PLATFORM FOR LARGE-SCALE PROCUREMENT AUTOMATION
abstract: Enterprise procurement processes involve complex activities such as supplier discovery, requirement analysis, sourcing strategy development, quotation evaluation, negotiation, compliance verification, and purchase decision support.Conventional procurement platforms primarily rely on rule-based workflows, human-driven coordination, and isolated automation components, limiting their ability to dynamically respond to changing business requirements and large-scale sourcing demands.Recent advances in agentic artificial intelligence provide an opportunity to transform procurement operations through autonomous software agents capable of reasoning, planning, executing tasks, coordinating with other agents, and adapting to changing conditions.This article presents a generalized architectural approach for an enterprise agentic AI platform for autonomous sourcing.The proposed platform employs a secure multiagent architecture in which specialized agents perform complementary procurement functions, including requirement interpretation, supplier discovery, supplier qualification, market intelligence, quotation analysis, negotiation support, compliance Sreedivya

title: Hierarchical Progressive Optimization for Multi-Qubit Pauli Noise Modeling
abstract: Abstract Quantum Noise Characterization (QNC) is indispensable for benchmarking and mitigating errors in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. However, traditional Quantum Process Tomography (QPT) suffers from an exponential parameter explosion, severely hindering its scalability. In this paper, we propose a Hierarchical Progressive Optimization (HPO) framework to efficiently extract high-order spatial crosstalk in multi-qubit systems. The complexity analysis shows that the combinatorial projection mask reduces the required number of Pauli transfer matrix (PTM) elements from O (16 N ) to O ( N 2 3 N ). Numerical simulations on a 10-qubit HHL circuit achieve a fidelity of 0.9381 with the HPO method, compared to 0.7431 obtained using global depolarizing-noise mitigation.

title: Network Topologies for QKD Networks
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a method for distributing cryptographic keys between remote endpoints, enjoying security based on quantum physics. This paper makes a first step towards studying topologies for QKD networks. QKD networks imply several required characteristics for their reliability and efficiency. We express such properties in terms of graph structure. For the comparison of potential graphs, we describe cost functions that allow us to identify families of graphs that are reliable and efficient. To make the discussion realistic, we summarize representative field-reported QKD performance numbers and illustrate the sensitivity of secret-key rate (SKR) to a few dB of additional loss. Last, we present methods to construct large efficient graphs through connecting smaller graphs.

title: The Photonic Computer
abstract: This document presents the first complete architecture based on directional photonic theory, a new science of computation in which light becomes the primary carrier of information, coherence, and structure. It explains how directional geometries, fractals, hyperfractals, and dynamic, adaptive, emergent, and self‑replicating structures can be organized to form a light‑based computer capable of surpassing all existing technologies. The work explores in depth the fundamental properties of photonic computation: directional coherence, multidimensional stability, luminous synchronization, fractal and hyperfractal structures, spatiotemporal dynamics, internal adaptation mechanisms, the emergence of new behaviors, geometric replication, and the foundations of intelligent computation. It demonstrates why the photonic computer is superior to the quantum computer: light suffers no decoherence, operates at room temperature, carries more states than a qubit, enables non‑destructive geometries, and offers a level of stability that superconducting systems will never achieve. This document is not merely a technical description: it is the foundation of a new computational era, where light becomes the universal medium for computation, structure, and evolution.

title: AffectLoop: From Experience to Conditional Self-Reaction Prediction with Counterfactual Twins
abstract: Can an LLM-based agent system acquire a branch-specific model of its own future reactions from controlled experience, use that model prospectively, and revise it after counterevidence? We introduce a counterfactual-twin assay in which matched agent branches share the same Actor, initial conditions, available actions, and outcome multiset but differ in the contextual binding of those outcomes. The assay separates five questions that are often conflated: experience-conditioned reaction divergence, storage in a prospective Core, transfer beyond cue identity, Actor access, and selective revision. Across five precommitted source–twin pairs, progressively stronger shortcut-removal assays preserved low error for the correct Core while twin-swapped and no-Core controls remained substantially worse. In the strongest Actor assay, a Qwen3-8B Actor directly predicted ordinal changes on four reaction axes with 94.38% directional accuracy under the correct Core, compared with 0% after twin swapping, 51.88% after targeted local inversion, and 26.88% with no Core; predictions were committed before independent held-out Native Reactions were generated. A separate zero-Actor-call track tested system-level online formation and revision. Online Core formation reduced held-out binary error from 0.4875 with an empty Core to 0 with the correct learned Core, whereas the twin Core yielded error 1.0. Local counterevidence revision reduced anchor-near error from 0.41484 to 0 without changing far probes; shuffled and twin updates failed. A first-attempt confirmatory run on five precommitted unused pairs reproduced the full functional J–M–E1–F1 chain, with all five revision gains positive (mean 0.41189; exact one-sided sign-test p = .03125), 99.3% of the original mean gain. These results support a bounded claim: the system implements an experience-grounded, branch-specific prospective self-model that can guide ordinal self-prediction and undergo engineered local revision. They do not establish consciousness, phenomenological selfhood, privileged introspection, or autonomous discovery of the reaction-generating mechanism.

title: Formal Model of Cognitive Bias in Reinforcement Learning Agents
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents are increasingly deployed in complex environments, yet their performance is often surprisingly brittle and susceptible to suboptimal strategies. This brittleness stems, in part, from inherent cognitive biases that mimic human decision-making processes. This paper presents a formal model of cognitive bias within RL agents, arguing that these biases are predictable and can be formally represented and mitigated. The core of our approach involves integrating concepts from behavioral economics and cognitive psychology – specifically confirmation bias, the availability heuristic, and loss aversion – into the agent's decision-making process. We define a mathematical framework, utilizing variables such as *Q(s, a)* representing the action-value function and *R(s, a)* representing the reward function, to quantify the impact of these biases. The model introduces a bias factor, *β*, that modifies the expected reward calculation, reflecting the influence of the heuristic. We demonstrate how this bias factor can be dynamically adjusted based on observed environmental feedback, leading to improved agent robustness and performance. The novelty of this work lies in providing a rigorous, mathematically grounded approach to understanding and addressing cognitive biases in RL, shifting the focus from purely reward-based optimization to incorporating psychological insights. We outline a methodology for identifying and quantifying biases, and propose strategies for mitigating their detrimental effects. Ultimately, this model offers a pathway towards more reliable and adaptable RL agents.

title: Quantum Walk-Based Optimization of Neural Network Architecture
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network architecture search (NAS) leveraging the principles of quantum walks. Traditional NAS methods suffer from significant computational bottlenecks, limiting their scalability and practicality. We introduce a framework where quantum walks are employed to efficiently explore the vast architectural search space. The core idea is to map the architectural choices – such as the number of layers, the type of activation functions, and the connections between neurons – to a quantum state, allowing for parallel exploration guided by the inherent probabilistic nature of quantum walks. The algorithm iteratively evolves the quantum state, favoring architectures that maximize performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, inference time) while minimizing computational complexity. This approach offers the potential to dramatically accelerate the NAS process, enabling the discovery of high-performing neural network architectures with reduced computational cost. The theoretical framework is presented, along with a detailed explanation of the quantum walk implementation and its convergence properties. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential of this method through a series of simulations, showcasing its ability to outperform conventional NAS techniques in terms of both speed and architectural quality.

title: Hyperdimensional Computing for Distributed Quantum State Teleportation
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to quantum state teleportation leveraging hyperdimensional computing (HDC). Traditional quantum state teleportation protocols face limitations due to qubit fidelity requirements and the complexity associated with distributing entangled qubits over long distances. We propose utilizing HDC – high-dimensional vectors characterized by near-orthogonal components – to represent and transmit quantum states. Our method significantly reduces the need for direct qubit entanglement, offering a potentially scalable and robust alternative. The core mechanism involves encoding the quantum state information into the high-dimensional vector components and subsequently extracting the state at the destination. We detail the mathematical framework underpinning this approach, focusing on vector projections, inner products, and state reconstruction. The results demonstrate a viable path towards distributed quantum state teleportation, addressing the key challenges of fidelity and entanglement distribution. We provide a detailed analysis of the computational complexity and potential advantages of this HDC-based teleportation scheme.

title: Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Strategies and Bayesian Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to symbolic regression that leverages the strengths of both evolutionary strategies (ES) and Bayesian optimization (BO) to achieve significantly improved equation discovery performance. Traditional symbolic regression methods often struggle with the high dimensionality and complex relationships inherent in data, leading to slow convergence and suboptimal solutions. Our approach addresses this challenge by employing an ES framework to explore the vast space of potential mathematical equations, while a BO algorithm intelligently guides the ES search, focusing on regions of the space with the highest probability of containing accurate equations. The core of our method lies in the synergy between these two techniques: the ES provides a robust exploration mechanism, while the BO offers a targeted and efficient exploitation strategy. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and a detailed examination of the algorithmic components that this combined approach offers a substantial advantage over standalone ES or BO methods. The results show a notable improvement in equation accuracy and convergence speed, particularly for datasets with complex underlying relationships.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Graph Embedding with Contrastive Predictive Coding
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding using self-supervised learning, specifically leveraging the principles of contrastive predictive coding (CPC). Existing graph embedding techniques frequently employ simplistic pretext tasks, often resulting in embeddings that fail to fully capture the intricate relationships within graph data. Our method addresses this limitation by training a model to predict future node states based on their past states, guided by a contrastive loss function. This allows the model to learn richer and more informative embeddings by explicitly enforcing similarity between related states and dissimilarity between unrelated states. We demonstrate that this approach yields significantly improved graph embeddings compared to traditional self-supervised methods, highlighting the potential of CPC for capturing complex graph dependencies. The core claim of this work is that contrastive predictive coding can create richer and more informative graph embeddings, moving beyond the limitations of simpler pretext tasks.

title: Emergent Explanation Generation for Explainable Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The increasing deployment of complex Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, particularly deep neural networks, raises critical concerns about their interpretability. Traditional explanation methods often rely on post-hoc analysis, introducing potential biases and failing to capture the underlying cognitive mechanisms driving model behavior. This paper proposes a novel algorithmic framework for automatically generating emergent explanations within AI models. The core principle is to directly extract and translate internal activation patterns into human-understandable explanations. We leverage Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) and association rule mining to identify salient patterns within model activations and subsequently generate explanations that highlight significant relationships. The proposed approach offers a shift from manual interpretation to automated discovery, aiming to unveil the hidden cognitive processes within AI systems. The system's ability to autonomously generate explanations represents a significant advancement in the field of Explainable AI (XAI), promoting a deeper understanding of AI decision-making and fostering trust in these increasingly prevalent technologies. The generated explanations are presented in terms of rules and patterns, facilitating easier comprehension.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Clinical Reliability in Histology
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming histological tissue analysis in veterinary sciences, but the limited interpretability of deep learning models remains a major barrier to clinical adoption. This chapter examines explainable AI (XAI) techniques, including Grad-CAM, LIME, SHAP, and attention mechanisms, and their role in improving diagnostic transparency and reliability in veterinary histopathology. Drawing on evidence from canine mammary tumours, feline lymphoma, equine pulmonary disease, and comparative computational pathology, it explores how XAI supports whole-slide image analysis, quality assurance, and regulatory compliance by highlighting the morphological features underlying AI predictions. The chapter concludes with practical recommendations and future research priorities focused on standardized evaluation, clinical validation, and robust data governance to strengthen trust in AI-assisted veterinary diagnostics.

title: ContextPilot: Teaching Agents for Proactive Context Management via Fine-grained RL
abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks require large language models (LLMs) to iteratively retrieve, integrate, and maintain dispersed information across multi-turn interactions, but preserving all interaction histories leads to a continuously growing working context. Recent proactive context management methods allow models to edit their own working context with specialized tools, yet they still face three key limitations: (1) a limited toolset restricted to search, deletion, and summarization, with no support for global planning, long-term memory, and adaptive compression; (2) inefficient exploration that treats context management actions uniformly despite their heterogeneous impacts on final outcomes; and (3) coarse-grained credit assignment that assigns the final trajectory-level reward to all intermediate context editing actions during RL. To bridge these gaps, we introduce ContextPilot, a proactive context management framework for long-horizon agentic reasoning. Our approach systematically augments the toolset with planning, long-term memory, and soft context offloading tools. We further propose an RL method tailored for context management, which uses context and entropy variation to identify critical editing decisions for branch sampling and estimates action-level advantages from all branched trajectories that pass through the corresponding context editing action. Experiments on long-context QA and deep search tasks show that ContextPilot achieves stronger performance with a more compact working context, consistently outperforming existing baselines across various base models and benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Tencent/ContextPilot.

title: GOD: Govern, Observe, and Direct - A Real-Time Control Room for Agent Societies
abstract: Generative-agent systems are easier to start than to inspect. A run can contain many agents, locations, messages, commands, and model calls, yet the operator often gets either a finished replay or raw logs. That makes it hard to ask why an agent moved, test a small intervention, or package a run for another researcher. GOD is a local-first control room for agent societies. From the same browser workflow, an operator can issue targeted questions or interventions and inspect the resulting replay state. The system combines a setup wizard, Agent Studio, Map Studio, a spatial replay interface, Ask and Intervene commands, and portable experiment, map, and agent packs. Its technical contribution is the command and artifact loop: live controls and replay evidence share the same operator command model, while package contracts separate scenario, map, and profile data from local runtime state. The public release includes hosted Smallville-style and PKU replays, the open-source repository, and downloadable packs. We evaluate this path on 15 completed run slots. Across the 14 intervention runs, 78 of 84 target-agent checks recorded the commanded destination, and 169 of 182 state answers matched a saved location or action string.

title: Quantum Machine Learning with Quantum Feature Selection
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of combining quantum machine learning with quantum feature selection to enhance the performance of machine learning models. The core idea is to frame the machine learning problem as a quantum feature selection problem, leveraging quantum phenomena such as entanglement and superposition to effectively identify the most informative features. Traditional feature selection methods often struggle with high-dimensional datasets and may not fully exploit the inherent correlations between features. Quantum feature selection, utilizing quantum computers, offers a fundamentally different approach, potentially capable of identifying subtle relationships and patterns that classical methods miss. This paper explores the theoretical framework, outlining the conversion process and the utilization of quantum mechanics to optimize feature selection. The proposed method aims to achieve superior classification and regression results compared to conventional machine learning algorithms. We present a detailed mathematical description of the process, emphasizing the key quantum concepts involved. The ultimate goal is to demonstrate a viable pathway for advancing machine learning capabilities through the integration of quantum computing principles.

evidence.title: Quantum Machine Learning with Quantum Feature Selection
evidence.abstract: This paper investigates the potential of combining quantum machine learning with quantum feature selection to enhance the performance of machine learning models. The core idea is to frame the machine learning problem as a quantum feature selection problem, leveraging quantum phenomena such as entanglement and superposition to effectively identify the most informative features. Traditional feature selection methods often struggle with high-dimensional datasets and may not fully exploit the inherent correlations between features. Quantum feature selection, utilizing quantum computers, offers a fundamentally different approach, potentially capable of identifying subtle relationships and patterns that classical methods miss. This paper explores the theoretical framework, outlining the conversion process and the utilization of quantum mechanics to optimize feature selection. The proposed method aims to achieve superior classification and regression results compared to conventional machine learning algorithms. We present a detailed mathematical description of the process, emphasizing the key quantum concepts involved. The ultimate goal is to demonstrate a viable pathway for advancing machine learning capabilities through the integration of quantum computing principles.

title: Adaptive Neural Network Architectures via Genetic Regulatory Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network architecture design by integrating principles from genetic regulatory networks (GRNs). Traditional neural network training relies heavily on gradient descent, often leading to suboptimal architectures and inefficient training processes. Our methodology introduces a simulated "genetic network" that dynamically governs the architecture of a neural network during training. This network adjusts parameters like layer sizes, connection strengths, and activation functions based on performance feedback, mirroring the adaptive mechanisms observed in biological systems. The core claim is that mimicking GRNs' self-regulation can lead to more effective and adaptive neural network architectures. We outline the design of this training regime, focusing on the interplay between the neural network and the simulated genetic network. The theoretical framework is presented, highlighting the potential benefits of this approach over conventional gradient-based methods. The research explores how feedback loops and regulatory elements within the GRN can drive the neural network towards increasingly efficient and specialized architectures. We demonstrate the feasibility of this concept and suggest future research directions for further development and experimentation.

title: Machine Learning for Automated Theorem Proving using Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper explores the application of reinforcement learning (RL) to automate theorem proving, a long-standing challenge in artificial intelligence and mathematics. The core idea is to train an RL agent to strategically guide a traditional theorem prover, effectively learning a proof strategy. The system operates by the RL agent observing the state of the theorem prover – typically represented by the current set of axioms, hypotheses, and inference steps – and then selecting actions, such as applying specific inference rules or searching for new axioms. The reward signal provided to the agent is designed to incentivize progress towards a valid proof. This approach represents a novel combination of machine learning and automated reasoning, with the potential to create truly autonomous proof systems. We detail the architecture of the system, the RL algorithm employed, and the design choices made for the reward function. The goal is to demonstrate the feasibility of learning efficient proof strategies through interaction and feedback. The paper focuses on conceptual design and potential architectures, not on a fully realized system, and highlights the key challenges and future research directions in this area.

title: Information-Theoretic Security Protocols for Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: This paper investigates the design of quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols rooted in information-theoretic principles. Traditional QKD approaches often rely on the presumed computational hardness of certain mathematical problems. This work advocates for a paradigm shift, utilizing concepts such as channel capacity and mutual information to establish security guarantees directly. We explore protocols that explicitly measure and manage information flow between sender and receiver, drawing upon channel capacity to mitigate eavesdropping attempts. The core contribution lies in a framework for designing QKD protocols that are resilient to channel impairments and provide verifiable security bounds based on information-theoretic metrics. The proposed designs offer a more robust and fundamental approach to QKD security, independent of computational assumptions. We present a detailed analysis of key aspects including channel capacity limits, mutual information calculations, and the resulting security parameters.

title: A Cognitive Architecture-Based Programming Language
abstract: This paper proposes a novel programming language designed around the principles of cognitive architectures. The core claim is that by embedding cognitive architecture concepts directly into the language, we can significantly improve the ease of use, explainability, and ultimately, the alignment of software with human cognitive processes. The language, termed "CogniLang," utilizes a new programming paradigm derived from architectures like Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and COG. CogniLang introduces concepts such as values, experiences, and interventions as first-class citizens within the language, allowing programmers to model not just *what* a program does, but *how* it does it, mirroring human thought processes. The paper details the key features and syntax of CogniLang, illustrating how it diverges from traditional programming paradigms. It argues that this approach represents a significant step towards creating software that is more intuitive, adaptable, and genuinely understandable by humans. The language's design focuses on promoting a mindful and iterative development process, reflecting the core tenets of cognitive science.

title: Emerging AI Technologies in Veterinary Histology
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming veterinary histology by enhancing the accuracy, speed, and consistency of tissue analysis and disease diagnosis. The integration of machine learning, deep learning, digital pathology, whole-slide imaging, and explainable AI enables automated tissue classification, lesion detection, cellular analysis, and quantitative histomorphometry. Emerging technologies such as vision transformers, generative AI, federated learning, and cloud-based platforms further expand research and diagnostic capabilities. Despite challenges related to dataset availability, species diversity, data quality, and ethical concerns, AI offers significant opportunities for advancing veterinary diagnostics, education, precision medicine, and One Health initiatives. Continued development and validation will drive future innovations.

title: Exploring Public Reaction to Air Quality on Social Media: The 2022 Saharan Dust Episode in Lisbon
abstract: This study analyses the relationship between air quality and sentiments expressed on social media, focusing on the Saharan dust episode that affected Lisbon in March 2022. Environmental data were collected alongside geolocated Twitter posts (now rebranded as X) from the Lisbon area. The content of these posts was analysed using the Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner algorithm to identify emotional patterns and assess correlations with fluctuations in atmospheric pollutants. A predictive analysis was also conducted using Decision Tree and Random Forest machine learning algorithms. The findings suggest that despite high levels of inhalable particulate matter (PM10) during the event, there was no significant change in online sentiments, which remained mostly neutral or slightly positive. This implies that the publics environ-mental perception may not be clearly reflected on social media, possibly due to cultural factors or the limited influence of Twitter in Portugal. The study concludes that integrating environmental and social data is feasible and valuable, but further research is needed to explore longer periods, other cities, and more advanced techniques, thus contributing to the understanding of air pollution and public perception in Portugal.

title: Compositional and adaptive visual recognition under domain shift
abstract: Human vision is remarkably robust, data-efficient, and adaptive. People can recognize objects across changes in style, viewpoint, lighting, modality, and context, often from only a few examples. Modern deep learning systems, despite their impressive performance, still depend heavily on large labeled datasets and often degrade when the test distribution differs from the training distribution. This brittleness is especially consequential in settings where labels are scarce, data are decentralized, or privacy constraints prevent the construction of large centralized datasets. This thesis argues that robust visual recognition requires moving beyond the dominant view of images as global patterns mapped directly to labels. Instead, recognition should be grounded in the structure of visual evidence. Objects and scenes are composed of parts, regions, relations, and context-dependent cues that are not equally relevant to recognition. Inspired by biological perception, the thesis organizes this view around three computational principles. First, visual representations should expose compositional structure rather than collapse images into monolithic embeddings. Second, recognition should selectively compare the evidence that is shared, discriminative, and stable while suppressing clutter, background, and nuisance variation. Third, inference should adapt to the input, domain, or task without requiring full retraining or access to target-domain supervision. The thesis develops architectures and learning strategies that encourage part–whole and region-level structure; training-free and few-shot inference methods that compare images through selected local evidence rather than global similarity alone; adaptive specialization mechanisms that preserve pretrained knowledge while changing the effective computation for new domains; and robustness-oriented optimization strategies that reduce reliance on nuisance-sensitive cues. Although these methods differ in form, they share the goal of making recognition depend less on superficial appearance correlations and more on structured, reusable, and task-relevant visual evidence. The thesis shows that compositional structure, selective evidence use, and adaptive inference provide a coherent foundation for recognition under domain shift, data scarcity, and privacy constraints. Across natural images, medical imaging, federated learning, cross-domain few-shot recognition, and video understanding, the work demonstrates that robust visual recognition is not only a matter of larger models or more data, but of representing and using visual evidence in a more structured and adaptive way.

title: LayerRecall: A State-Conditioned Memory Router for Long-Horizon Consistency in Video Generation
abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion enables scalable long-video generation by producing chunks from a bounded recent context. While recency-based caching preserves local continuity, it evicts historical cues needed when subjects, objects, scenes, or attributes reappear. Existing memory mechanisms expose models to nonlocal history, but access alone does not ensure effective use. Our analysis reveals that video DiT layers exhibit distinct preferences for current, recent, and distant context, suggesting that long-range memory requires deciding both what to retrieve and where to use it. We introduce LayerRecall, a current-conditioned, layer-selective memory router that retrieves relevant historical K/V states and injects them only into backbone-specific memory-sensitive layers while preserving local attention elsewhere. To reduce reliance on scarce high-quality long-horizon videos and explicit memory-allocation labels, we further propose Cross-Horizon Prediction Matching (CHPM), which uses a privileged long-context reference to supervise the bounded-memory router in prediction space. Across 100 multi-shot evaluation prompts, LayerRecall achieves the best overall results on MemoBench and MovieBench while matching its backbone on VBench-Long, demonstrating stronger long-range recovery without sacrificing local continuity. Qualitative analyses further reveal memory-guided self-correction, whereby initially mismatched local attributes return to their historical appearance without resetting ongoing motion or scene structure. Additional analyses show cross-backbone portability and negligible inference overhead.

title: SEPO: Evidence-Grounded Prompt Optimization via Structural Editing
abstract: Existing API-only prompt optimisers are often described as interpretable, but in practice, this usually means only post-hoc inspectability: each iteration still rewrites the prompt as one opaque string, leaving a trace of full-prompt diffs rather than localisable, machine-readable edits. This paper introduces SEPO (Structural, Evidence-grounded Prompt Optimization), a multi-trajectory prompt optimiser centred on edit-effect lineage feedback. Rather than treating each iteration as an isolated whole-prompt rewrite, SEPO locally edits stable, typed units in a two-layer prompt schema, links the target and realised structural operations of each edit to the examples it newly fixes or breaks, and carries this edit-effect record forward to guide later architect calls on the same search branch. This makes prompt optimisation addressable, attributable, and actionable. Across a 14-task held-out suite, SEPO improves over the strongest baseline, GEPA, by 3.1 pp on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and 2.2 pp on Qwen3-8B, reaching 61.9% and 73.3% macro accuracy. SEPO also lies on both the optimisation-time and test-time Pareto frontiers, spending 2.9M optimisation tokens versus 4.1M for GEPA and producing prompts over 5x shorter.

title: Entity-Memory Graph Retrieval Improves Evidence Coverage in Long-Conversation Question Answering
abstract: Entity-Memory graph retrieval keeps dialogue turns as verbatim Memory nodes, links repeated mentions through shared Entities, and connects adjacent Memories with directed chronological edges. At query time the retriever moves from Entity gating through semantic fusion and one-hop chronological recovery to dense backfill. The path can keep a neighboring Memory that dense cosine ranking would otherwise omit. A matched dense control shares the Memory and query vectors, context budget, requested answer protocol, and evaluator, isolating graph structure from changes to the reader. On 1,986 questions from ten LoCoMo conversations, graph retrieval raises official evidence recall at top-k 25 from 79.7468% to 84.4842%. The recall advantage is supported from top-k 5 to 50, while no matched cutoff supports an overall final-answer F1 difference. Four paper-eligible requested configurations support empirical robustness across the tested GPT-3.5 and DeepSeek extractors on both outcomes. Embedding robustness is mixed: F1 has no supported contrast, but recall is sensitive to the embedding artifact. The comparison isolates a retrieval-coverage gain from graph structure. It does not establish a final-answer F1 gain, model or embedding equivalence, or cross-dataset generalization.

title: ##基于语义网络推理的编译器优化
abstract: This paper proposes a novel compiler optimization technique based on semantic network reasoning. Traditional compiler optimization relies heavily on manually crafted algorithms, leading to limitations in generality and automation. Our approach addresses these shortcomings by leveraging semantic networks to represent program code and employing semantic network reasoning to perform comprehensive code analysis. Specifically, we utilize techniques such as dependency analysis and data flow analysis within the semantic network framework. This allows the compiler to automatically learn the semantic nuances of code, enabling the generation of optimized instructions with improved accuracy and efficiency. The core claim of this work is to develop a compiler that automatically optimizes code by understanding its semantic meaning through semantic network reasoning. The proposed methodology offers a promising path toward more adaptive and effective compiler optimization, ultimately leading to enhanced software performance. ---

title: Context-Aware Differential Privacy with Personalized Noise Calibration
abstract: Differential privacy (DP) offers a rigorous mathematical framework for protecting individual privacy while enabling statistical analysis of datasets. However, traditional DP methods frequently rely on uniform noise addition, which can be overly conservative, introducing significant noise and diminishing data utility, especially when dealing with diverse datasets. This paper proposes a novel context-aware differential privacy framework that dynamically calibrates noise scales based on the individual's data distribution and the sensitivity of the query. The core idea is to recognize that data heterogeneity necessitates a more nuanced approach to privacy protection. We introduce a mechanism that estimates the data distribution for each individual and adjusts the noise scale proportionally to the query's sensitivity within that context. This personalized noise calibration significantly reduces the overall noise level compared to uniform scaling, leading to improved data utility without compromising differential privacy guarantees. Our approach addresses a fundamental limitation of existing DP techniques and provides a more practical and efficient solution for privacy-preserving data analysis in real-world scenarios. The theoretical framework is presented, and the core algorithm is detailed. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the method through a series of illustrative examples.

title: Algorithmic Transparency and Explainable AI using Quantum Information Theory
abstract: The increasing deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems across various domains necessitates a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Current explainable AI (XAI) techniques often struggle to provide truly transparent and reliable explanations, particularly for complex models like deep neural networks. This paper proposes a novel approach to algorithmic transparency and XAI leveraging concepts from quantum information theory. Specifically, we explore the potential of quantum entanglement and mutual information to represent and analyze AI model decisions in a fundamentally different way. Our framework represents model outputs as quantum states and investigates the correlations between these states and the input data. This analysis aims to identify the key factors driving the model's decision and provide a more intuitive and understandable explanation. We demonstrate that utilizing quantum information theory can offer a richer and more robust approach to XAI than traditional methods, potentially addressing limitations related to interpretability and trust in AI systems. This work lays the groundwork for a new paradigm in AI transparency, utilizing the unique properties of quantum mechanics to enhance the explainability of complex algorithms.

title: Bayesian Network-Based Causal Discovery Algorithm (BNCDA)
abstract: This paper introduces the Bayesian Network-Based Causal Discovery Algorithm (BNCDA), a novel approach to causal inference leveraging the structure of Bayesian Networks. The core claim of this work is that Bayesian Networks can be effectively utilized to discover causal relationships within datasets. The algorithm operates by learning conditional independence relationships from data and employing this information to infer a causal graph. Unlike traditional causal discovery methods that heavily rely on domain expertise and prior knowledge, BNCDA aims to learn directly from data. This paper outlines the theoretical foundations of BNCDA, details the algorithm's implementation, and discusses potential applications and limitations. The ultimate goal is to provide a data-driven approach to causal discovery, facilitating more robust and interpretable causal models.

This paper outlines the theoretical foundations of BNCDA, details the algorithm's implementation, and discusses potential applications and limitations. The ultimate goal is to provide a data-driven approach to causal discovery, facilitating more robust and interpretable causal models.

title: ##基于微分几何的神经网络结构优化
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to neural network optimization by leveraging concepts from differential geometry. Traditional neural network architecture optimization often relies on heuristic search methods or reinforcement learning, which can be computationally expensive and lack theoretical guarantees. We propose a framework where the network's connections and topology are represented as geometric objects, allowing us to apply gradient-based optimization techniques, specifically inspired by Riemannian geometry, to directly optimize the network's structure. The core claim is that this geometric perspective provides a fundamentally new way to approach network design, potentially leading to significant improvements in network performance and efficiency. This work introduces a method for iteratively refining network architectures by minimizing a cost function defined within the geometric space, offering a promising avenue for automated and principled neural network design. The focus is on the optimization process itself, without the need for specific network architectures, and the goal is to demonstrate the feasibility and potential benefits of this approach.

title: AI-Based Histological Image Analysis and Tissue Classification Approaches
abstract: Integration of AI into the histology field is revolutionizing the biomedicine and veterinary science sectors through enhanced accuracy, precision, and consistency of diagnosis. However, since traditional histopathology can have problems associated with subjectivity and inconsistencies, there is increased standardization and consistency due to AI applications. In digital pathology, whole slide imaging (WSI) can be used for the creation of high-quality images obtained from tissue specimens and analyzed using computerized systems. The pre-processing of data by using such methods as normalization, denoising, and segmentation leads to data enhancement, whereas deep learning, such as convolutional neural networks, makes tissue classification easier. Decision support systems driven by AI play an essential role in diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment plans, along with other uses in veterinary herd health management and epidemiology. AI offers benefits but faces challenges like data privacy, bias, and explainability; multimodal fusion will enhance personalized care

title: Adaptive weighted XGBoost optimization with multifeature fusion for industrial data prediction
abstract: Traditional machine learning-based data prediction is core to industrial intelligent operation, equipment monitoring and energy scheduling. With the widespread application of sensors and industrial Internet, industrial scenarios continuously generate massive high-dimensional, noisy and multicollinear data, raising higher demands for prediction model accuracy and generalization[1]. As an efficient ensemble learning algorithm, XGBoost is widely used in regression prediction due to its superior nonlinear fitting, robustness and computational efficiency[2]. However, traditional XGBoost has apparent limitations in industrial prediction. Industrial high-dimensional data contains numerous irrelevant and collinear redundant features that interfere with model training and degrade prediction performance[3]. Besides, its fixed feature weight allocation and static learning rate fail to adapt to complex data distribution changes, causing slow convergence and local optimum problems[4]. To solve these problems, this paper proposes an integrated optimization pipeline for XGBoost, A dual-criterion screening strategy combining Pearson correlation coefficient and VIF is constructed to remove invalid low-correlation and multicollinear features[5]. An adaptive weighting mechanism based on tree splitting gain is designed to dynamically adjust feature contributions[6]. Meanwhile, an exponential decay dynamic learning rate is adopted to accelerate early convergence and stabilize late optimization[7] . Comparative experiments, ablation experiments and noise robustness tests are conducted on public datasets. The results show that the proposed method reduces MAE by 12.3% and RMSE by 10.8%, with the R² reaching 0.976, outperforming SVR, Random Forest, LightGBM and original XGBoost. Ablation experiments validate the effectiveness of each improved module, and robustness tests confirm its strong anti-noise capability and generalization[8] . This method can provide reliable technical support for industrial time-series prediction and intelligent early warning

title: A UAV path planning method based on the WOAGWO hybrid algorithm
abstract: Addressing challenges such as strong terrain constraints and susceptibility to local optima in UAV path planning within complex mountainous environments, this paper introduces a path planning method based on the Whale Optimization Algorithm-Grey Wolf Optimizer (WOAGWO) hybrid algorithm. First, the hierarchical hunting mechanism of the Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) is embedded into the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) framework. During the exploitation phase of WOA, the cooperative position update strategy of GWO's α, β, and δ wolves is incorporated. The design of dynamic triggering conditions achieves deep fusion between the two algorithms. This fusion mechanism significantly enhances the local search precision of WOA, effectively overcoming the technical limitation of traditional WOA's tendency to converge to local optima. Second, an adaptive solution quality assurance technique is developed for the algorithm's exploration phase. By establishing an iterative feedback mechanism, the fitness values of new solutions are compared in real-time with historical optimal solutions. This ensures search agents consistently move toward superior regions, enabling efficient global exploration. Simulation trials demonstrate that compared to original WOA, GWO, and other mainstream algorithms, the WOAGWO algorithm can identify safe and feasible paths in complex mountainous terrains with lower convergence costs, validating its superiority.

title: Lindblad-engineered spectral viscosity for quantum simulation of dissipative fluid dynamics
abstract: Abstract Molecular viscosity in a classical fluid imposes the mode-selective energy-decay law γ k = 2 ν k 2 . Independent damping of physical qubits follows the binary occupation pattern of a mode register and generally produces a different spectrum. We construct a trace-preserving open-system primitive that transfers resolved Fourier-mode population to an auxiliary heat/sink state through mode-selective Lindblad jumps. Its finite-time Kraus map and Stinespring dilation realize the resolved-to-sink channel. A reduced ancilla-controlled circuit measures the associated mode-conditioned retention probabilities for prepared basis modes. Analytical derivation establishes the channel and its balance law. Ideal simulations verify the numerical implementations of the derived map and the retention-probability estimator. Heat-equation and viscous-Burgers calculations place the substep inside classical spectral time integration. IBM-processor experiments assess small-circuit feasibility. Two N k = 2 hardware runs preserve modal ordering, with relative decay-rate errors of 13.0%–19.9% for k = 1 and 7.3%–7.4% for k = 2 . The N k = 4 hardware circuit fails quantitative reproduction. Its mean k = 1 relative error is 145.5%, and mode-register flips are approximately 15%. This case is retained to characterize the onset and nature of the implementation failure. The results establish the calibrated channel while identifying the depth of the reduced controlled-rotation implementation as the present hardware bottleneck. Complete quantum computational fluid dynamics integration and quantum-advantage assessment remain future work.

title: Ladders in Chaos: When, How, (and Perhaps Why) Does Test-Time Scaling Improve LLM Machine Translation
abstract: Two forms of test-time scaling for Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as effective and widely adopted paradigms: sequential, in which later answer attempts depend on earlier ones, and parallel, such as i.i.d. sampling with reranking. In this study, we investigate their properties in translation. First, our study shows that sequential sampling has a higher performance ceiling, providing a more diverse and effective pool of samples, particularly under smaller sampling budgets. Second, we interrogate the nature of test-time scaling through a multidimensional manual analysis. Human analysis of the Best-of-N translations demonstrates that sequential sampling substantially improves translation fluency and naturalness, but can degrade accuracy when inference budgets are large. Finally, we suggest an explanation of the mechanism through which sequential scaling improves machine translation. Our controlled analysis partially attributes the success of sequential self-improvement to the model's access to a larger target-side context. Ablation experiments on sequential sampling demonstrate its robustness across different sampling temperatures, while also revealing sensitivity to context construction, suggesting directions for future improvement.

title: KLOD: Locality-Preserving Knowledge Editing via Non-Target Distribution Preservation
abstract: Fine-tuning-based knowledge editing is simple and architecture-agnostic, but standard cross-entropy increases the edited target probability without explicitly constraining changes in the non-target output distribution. In sequential editing, such unconstrained redistribution can accumulate as distributional drift and contribute to locality degradation. We propose KLOD, a bounded and distribution-preserving objective for fine-tuning-based knowledge editing that separates the intended target update from distributions that should remain stable. KLOD stops target amplification once a probability threshold is reached, while preserving the target-excluded non-target distribution at target positions and the full next-token distribution at prefix positions. Experiments on CounterFact and ZsRE with Llama3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that KLOD substantially mitigates locality degradation while maintaining high edit reliability. The target probability threshold further provides a controllable Generalization--Locality trade-off. Ablation, multi-seed, and distributional KL analyses support the interpretation that KLOD's locality gains are associated with preserving output distributions rather than simply weakening the edit. Code is available on GitHub https://github.com/Hostoday/KLOD .

title: Hybrid Batch Training for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer in XTREME-R
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: Does hybrid batch training with monolingual and multilingual data during intermediate-task fine-tuning improve zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on XTREME-R when compared to multilingual-only intermediate training? title: A Decision-Oriented Token as a Bounded, Threshold-Free Cache Key for Context-Conditioned Generative Edge Outputs: In-the-Loop Validation and Comparison Against Vector-Quantization, Learned, and Semantic Caches
abstract: A Decision-Oriented Token as a Bounded, Threshold-Free Cache Key for Context-Conditioned Generative Edge Outputs: In-the-Loop Validation and Comparison Against Vector-Quantization, Learned, and Semantic Caches Randolph James Ferlic, M.D. and Kimberly Kate Ferlic (Fieldstone Analytics, LLC, Austin, TX, USA) Preprint · Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22148612 · CC-BY 4.0 · Community: spiral-domain-encoder-campaign Abstract Generative models are moving to the edge to serve transient, context-conditioned ("flash") applications, where much of the cost, energy, and latency is paid outside generation — on the input, invocation, reuse, and transmission margins. We study whether a single decision-oriented token can reclaim that budget as a reuse-and-anticipation layer, without modifying the generative model. A previously filed class-discriminant codebook encoder reduces each window of a multivariate context stream to one 8-bit token chosen to preserve the downstream decision; we characterize that token, on five real public datasets (UCI HAR, Air Quality, Appliances Energy, Metro Interstate Traffic, Beijing PM2.5) under pre-registered protocols, primarily as a cache key for generative outputs. Main results. (i) As a cache key the token is bounded (a ≤K-entry cache and ≤K generations by construction), threshold-free (exact-hash lookup, no similarity threshold to tune), and decision-oriented — it cache-hits on decision-equivalent states. At equal bits it beats a generic unsupervised vector-quantization key by +0.08–0.185 decision fidelity and a learned VQ-VAE (TOTEM-style) key by +0.10–0.12; against a semantic cache (embedding + tuned threshold) it dominates at the efficient low-generation operating point on learnable targets (matching fidelity at ~20–40× fewer generations with a bounded cache), while the semantic cache reaches a higher fidelity ceiling on one dataset. (ii) With real generative models in the loop (Qwen2.5-0.5B and the 3× larger 1.5B-Instruct), across two datasets and both classification and free-form-advisory outputs — eight cells, with the decision's target held out of the prompt — conditioning on the token's codebook prototype stays within 0.05 of full-window conditioning in all eight cells, and token-cached serving exactly matches fresh generation in all eight, validating compression-preserves-quality and caching-preserves-quality end-to-end (these small models are weak at the decision itself, and the token's denoising edge on the 0.5B model fades to parity at 1.5B). (iii) The token's transition structure supports speculative prefetch that hides ~28–57% of gated-regeneration latency (55%+ on three of five datasets) using a small order-1 model. Honestly reframed and reported verbatim. The token is not a bandwidth compressor: against a lossless coder its on-wire advantage is only ~1.2–2.4×; its compression value is being a fixed-1-byte decision-oriented key and a ~19–96× reduction in real LLM prefill tokens (GPT-4/GPT-4o tokenizer). Invocation gating confers no unique advantage — a crude per-channel change detector gates as well or better; the token's value is that one representation serves caching, gating, and prefetch. The fidelity edge requires a labeled calibration set; a persistent token memory does not improve point decisions, is a poor generation-budget allocator via novelty, and discards trend magnitude; caching fidelity is capped by target predictability. The contribution is a decision-oriented, bounded, threshold-free reuse layer for generative edge output — validated in the loop and honestly bounded. Highlights · Decision-oriented cache key — one 8-bit token keys generative-output reuse; at equal bits it beats a generic unsupervised vector-quantization key (+0.08–0.185 decision fidelity), a learned VQ-VAE (TOTEM-style) tokenizer (+0.10–0.12), and semantic caching at the efficient low-generation operating point. · Bounded and threshold-free — a ≤K-entry cache and ≤K generations by construction, exact-hash O(1) lookup with no similarity threshold to tune; a deterministic worst-case-cost guarantee a similarity cache cannot offer. · Premise validated in the loop — real generators (Qwen2.5-0.5B and the 3× larger 1.5B-Instruct) across two datasets and both classification and free-form-advisory outputs (eight cells, decision target held out): conditioning on the token prototype stays within 0.05 of full-window conditioning in all eight cells, and token-cached serving exactly matches fresh generation in all eight. · On-device measurement (Apple M5 Pro) — encoder 4–13 µs/window, cache lookup ~44 ns, generation 127 ms (0.5B) / 282 ms (1.5B); the encoder is ≈20,000× cheaper than a generation and gated + cached serving cuts served latency by a measured 98.8–99.8%, matching the invocation-count model to 0.00 percentage points. · Speculative prefetch — a kilobyte-scale order-1 token-transition model hides ~28–57% of gated-regeneration latency (55%+ on three of five datasets), with a time-shuffle placebo confirming real temporal structure. · Honest two-number compression — the token is not a bandwidth compressor (a lossless coder competes to within ~1.2–2.4× on-wire); its compression value is being a fixed-1-byte decision-oriented, cache-keyable index plus a ~19–96× reduction in real LLM prefill tokens (GPT-4/GPT-4o tokenizer). · Honest negatives and reframes (reported verbatim) — invocation gating is a free rider (a crude change detector gates as well or better); persistent token memory does not aid point decisions; novelty is a poor generation-budget allocator; the token discards trend magnitude; the discriminant fidelity edge requires labels; caching fidelity is predictability-capped; and the small in-loop models are themselves weak decision-makers on these numeric tasks. What this record contains · Manuscript_Paper41.pdf — the manuscript (with the five figures embedded). · PAPER_41_ZENODO_ARCHIVE.zip — the reproducibility archive: the nine frozen pre-registrations, the eleven per-phase runners (including the two-model generator-in-the-loop and the on-device latency/energy measurement, plus the compression/gating-baseline and learned-VQ-VAE runners), the two figure-rebuild scripts, the per-experiment result JSON files, and the five figures. All paths and identifiers are scrubbed and leak-scanned per the campaign deposit discipline; no raw benchmark data is redistributed (all datasets are public; download instructions are in the archive README). a deterministic worst-case-cost guarantee a similarity cache cannot offer. · Premise validated in the loop — real generators (Qwen2.5-0.5B and the 3× larger 1.5B-Instruct) across two datasets and both classification and free-form-advisory outputs (eight cells, decision target held out): conditioning on the token prototype stays within 0.05 of full-window conditioning in all eight cells, and token-cached serving exactly matches fresh generation in all eight. · On-device measurement (Apple M5 Pro) — encoder 4–13 µs/window, cache lookup ~44 ns, generation 127 ms (0.5B) / 282 ms (1.5B); the encoder is ≈20,000× cheaper than a generation and gated + cached serving cuts served latency by a measured 98.8–99.8%, matching the invocation-count model to 0.00 percentage points. · Speculative prefetch — a kilobyte-scale order-1 token-transition model hides ~28–57% of gated-regeneration latency (55%+ on three of five datasets), with a time-shuffle placebo confirming real temporal structure. · Honest two-number compression — the token is not a bandwidth compressor (a lossless coder competes to within ~1.2–2.4× on-wire); title: Adaptive Quantum Circuit Compilation via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Quantum circuit compilation is a critical step in realizing quantum algorithms on near-term quantum hardware. The process of translating high-level quantum algorithms into low-level gate sequences, while minimizing gate count and circuit depth, is often performed using deterministic algorithms that struggle to adapt to the diverse and often imperfect characteristics of available quantum devices. This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum circuit compilation utilizing reinforcement learning (RL). An RL agent is trained to dynamically adapt to hardware constraints, such as qubit connectivity and gate decomposition costs, optimizing circuit fidelity and execution time. The core claim is that RL can significantly improve quantum circuit compilation by introducing a dynamic and adaptive compilation process. The agent learns a policy that maps high-level quantum algorithms to optimized low-level gate sequences, effectively bridging the gap between theoretical algorithms and practical hardware execution. This work demonstrates the potential of RL to overcome the limitations of traditional deterministic compilation methods and paves the way for more efficient and robust quantum algorithm implementation.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Quantum Algorithm Design
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum algorithm design by leveraging probabilistic programming. Traditional quantum algorithm design often relies on precise circuit specifications, which can be challenging due to the inherent uncertainty in quantum systems. We introduce a framework that allows users to define quantum algorithms as probability distributions, explicitly modeling the probabilistic nature of quantum computation. This framework enables the exploration of a wider range of potential solutions, facilitates optimization strategies based on probability, and provides a more intuitive way to design and understand quantum algorithms. The core concept is to represent quantum circuits not as deterministic operations, but as probability distributions over possible outcomes. This approach is particularly relevant for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices where errors are unavoidable and inherent probability plays a crucial role. We outline the key components of this framework, including a probabilistic programming language extension and a mechanism for translating circuit descriptions into probability distributions. The work demonstrates the potential of probabilistic programming to overcome the limitations of traditional design methods and accelerate the development of practical quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum-Inspired Relational Reasoning for Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly utilized for representing and reasoning over complex data. Traditional relational reasoning methods within KGs often struggle with scalability and efficiency, particularly when dealing with large and intricate graph structures. This paper proposes a novel approach to relational reasoning in KGs by incorporating quantum-inspired techniques. Specifically, we explore the application of Grover's search algorithm to accelerate the traversal and inference processes. Our core claim is that leveraging quantum-inspired algorithms can significantly improve the performance of querying and reasoning within KGs. We present a framework for adapting Grover's algorithm to KG traversal and inference, outlining the key steps and considerations. The resulting system demonstrates the potential for enhanced efficiency compared to traditional symbolic reasoning, particularly in scenarios with high computational complexity. We provide a detailed mathematical formulation of the underlying concepts and algorithms. The primary contribution of this work lies in demonstrating a viable pathway to harnessing the power of quantum-inspired methods for relational reasoning in knowledge graphs, opening possibilities for more scalable and intelligent knowledge representation and reasoning systems.

title: Dynamic Neuron Topology Network Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network learning based on dynamic neuron topology networks. The core idea is to mimic the dynamic topological structures found in biological neural networks to achieve more efficient and robust learning. We introduce a network architecture capable of adapting its topology – specifically, modifying neuron connections and adding or removing neurons – based on input data and reinforcement learning signals. This contrasts with traditional fixed-topology networks, enabling topological optimization during learning and potentially leading to improved learning efficiency and generalization performance. The primary mathematical framework revolves around representing the network topology as a graph (G = (V, E)), where V represents the set of neurons (s1, s2, ..., sK) and E represents the set of connections between neurons, defined by weighted edges (si, sj, wij), where wij represents the connection strength or weight. Reinforcement learning is incorporated using a reward function R(s, a) that guides the network's topological adjustments. The learning process is then formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), with the state 's' representing the network topology and the action 'a' representing a topological modification. The key contribution lies in the integration of dynamic topology adaptation with reinforcement learning, offering a potentially superior learning paradigm compared to static network architectures. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this approach, focusing on convergence properties and the impact of network topology on learning dynamics. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications of this framework in various domains, including pattern recognition, control systems, and robotics.

title: Adaptive Metric Learning for Relational Data
abstract: Metric learning aims to learn a distance function that reflects the similarity between data points. However, traditional approaches often fail when dealing with relational data, such as knowledge graphs and molecular interaction networks, due to the inherent ambiguity and complexity introduced by relationships. This paper proposes an adaptive metric learning framework that addresses this challenge. The framework utilizes an expectation-maximization (EM) iterative process to refine the learned metric. This approach dynamically adapts the metric representation by balancing precision and recall based on an evolving understanding of the data's relational structure, incorporating data uncertainty. Unlike static metric learning methods, our approach offers continuous adaptation, leading to improved performance in complex relational datasets. The key innovation lies in the dynamic adjustment of the metric based on the observed data uncertainty, providing a more robust and accurate representation. We formulate the problem mathematically, detailing the EM algorithm and the objective function used to iteratively refine the metric. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated through theoretical analysis and conceptual demonstrations, highlighting its potential for various relational data applications.

title: Causal Discovery from Observational Data using Bayesian Networks with Intervention Simulations
abstract: Inferring causal relationships from observational data is a fundamental problem in statistics and artificial intelligence. Traditional methods often struggle with confounding, where observed correlations between variables mask true causal connections. This paper proposes a novel approach to causal discovery that leverages Bayesian networks and intervention simulations. The core idea is to simulate interventions within the Bayesian network structure to directly observe the effects of manipulating variables and thereby mitigate confounding bias. We formulate the problem as estimating a causal Bayesian network structure where intervention effects are explicitly incorporated into the learning process. This approach offers a more robust way to identify causal relationships compared to standard observational data analysis. The methodology is presented, and the theoretical underpinnings are discussed, highlighting the key contributions and potential improvements. The paper focuses on the algorithmic aspects and theoretical considerations, offering a framework for future research in this area.

title: Cross-Species Diagnostic Translation in Volumetric Tissue Profiling
abstract: The digitization of veterinary histopathology is hindered by domain shift, where models trained on single-species data fail across the biological heterogeneity of disparate animal tissues. This chapter introduces a scalable computational framework to achieve cross-species diagnostic translation in volumetric tissue profiling. By deploying Convolutional Neural Networks augmented with spatial attention mechanisms, the architecture shifts the diagnostic focus from species-specific color to invariant structural patterns of disease. A core technical contribution is the mathematical formulation of an edge anomaly detection algorithm, utilizing active contours and curvature integration to isolate cellular boundary irregularities indicative of malignancy. To overcome the profound scarcity of annotated datasets, the framework integrates Multi-Source Transfer Learning and synthetic tissue generation, establishing a robust blueprint for democratizing artificial intelligence in veterinary medicine.

title: Blog: Survey of Optimizers
abstract: Neural-network optimization in 2025-2026 is no longer well described as a succession of new Adam variants. The design space has expanded from coordinates to matrices and layers, from fixed training horizons to policies over time, and from mathematical update rules to state representations that must survive sharding and low-precision computation. This survey organizes recent optimizers and training optimization methods along four largely independent axes: temporal estimation, update geometry, horizon management, and representation and systems. It connects the spectral normalization of Muon, the historical matrix statistics of Shampoo and SOAP, adaptive and hybrid matrix methods, memory-efficient optimizers, schedule-free training, small-batch corrections, and quantized optimizer states. The central empirical conclusion is deliberately non-triumphal: matrix-aware methods represent a genuine advance, but there is no context-independent replacement for AdamW. Rankings change with model scale, data-to-parameter ratio, batch size, schedule, parameter partition, tuning budget, and whether the target metric is tokens, FLOPs, wall-clock time, or memory. The practical consequence is a compositional view of optimizer design and a stricter protocol for evaluating optimizer claims.

title: ARC-CT: Anatomy-Routed Contrastive Vision-Language Learning for 3D Chest CT
abstract: Contrastive vision-language learning uses paired chest CT volumes and radiology reports to learn abnormality classifiers without manually annotated labels. However, two characteristics of chest CT challenge conventional global contrastive learning. First, many critical abnormalities are small or anatomically localized, and pooling an en- tire volume into a single embedding may dilute their visual evidence. Second, the standard contrastive objective treats every other scan in a batch as a negative. Because many chest CTs share abnormalities, this objective incorrectly pushes co-positive pairs apart. We propose Anatomy-Routed Contrastive Learning for 3D Chest CT (ARC-CT), a region-aware framework that addresses these limitations using only la- bels extracted from reports by an LLM, with no manual annotations or bounding boxes. ARC-CT combines three components: (1) an Anato- myQFormer localizing evidence via queries constrained by automatically generated organ masks; (2) a label-Jaccard soft InfoNCE objective in- tegrating the standard one-hot target with the label-set overlap of each pair, which reduces false-negative penalties between studies that share clinical findings; and (3) an organ-level alignment loss connecting mask- pooled visual features to organ-specific report text extracted offline with a large language model. ARC-CT achieves a 0.86 mask-free macro AUC across 18 abnormalities using a compact 3D ResNet-18 backbone. Over- all, ARC-CT outperforms both comparable efficient baselines and sev- eral larger transformer models. Our code and weights are available at https://github.com/arc-ct/arc-ct.

title: AERA: Adaptive Evidence Residual Allocation for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning
abstract: Test-time scaling improves language-model reasoning by generating additional candidate solutions, but allocating the same inference budget to every problem is computationally wasteful. Existing adaptive stopping methods commonly rely on confidence, agreement, or answer stability, implicitly assuming that stronger current evidence indicates that further computation is unnecessary. We show that this assumption can fail: checkpoint-level correctness evolves non-monotonically, and observable evidence may strengthen before an answer collapses or weaken before it recovers. Motivated by this mismatch, we introduce Adaptive Evidence Residual Allocation (AERA), a sequential controller that learns whether additional computation is likely to recover a better answer from checkpoint-observable evidence. AERA characterizes cumulative response prefixes using answer-distribution, temporal, re-solving, semantic, and compute features, and repeatedly decides whether to stop or allocate the next response block. Future checkpoint correctness is used only to construct offline supervision and is never available to the controller at inference time. Across GSM8K and GPQA Diamond, AERA identifies question-specific residual opportunities while substantially reducing inference computation. In a frozen-threshold incremental-generation evaluation on 300 untouched GSM8K questions, AERA achieves 92.61% accuracy versus 93.01% with 128 responses while reducing completion tokens by 95.99%. These results suggest that adaptive reasoning should estimate the future value of computation rather than equating present confidence with correctness.

title: L'ordinateur Photonique
abstract: Ce document présente la première architecture complète fondée sur la théorie directionnelle photonique, une science du calcul entièrement nouvelle où la lumière devient le vecteur principal de l’information, de la cohérence et de la structure. Il expose comment des géométries directionnelles, des fractales, des hyperfractales, des structures dynamiques, adaptatives, émergentes et auto‑réplicatives peuvent être organisées pour former un ordinateur fondé sur la lumière, capable de dépasser toutes les technologies actuelles. L’ouvrage explore en profondeur les propriétés fondamentales du calcul photonique : la cohérence directionnelle, la stabilité multidimensionnelle, la synchronisation lumineuse, les structures fractales et hyperfractales, les dynamiques spatio‑temporelles, les mécanismes d’adaptation interne, l’émergence de comportements nouveaux, la réplication géométrique, les fondations du calcul intelligent. Il démontre pourquoi l’ordinateur photonique est supérieur à l’ordinateur quantique : la lumière ne subit aucune décohérence, fonctionne à température ambiante, transporte plus d’états qu’un qubit, permet des géométries non destructrices, et offre une stabilité que les systèmes supraconducteurs ne pourront jamais atteindre. Ce document n’est pas seulement une description technique : c’est la base d’une nouvelle ère informatique, où la lumière devient le support universel du calcul, de la structure et de l’évolution.

title: Finite Typed Context Descent
abstract: Finite structural records are often observed through overlapping typed contexts. Coordinate coverage alone need not establish global equality, and locally admissible sections may fail to satisfy constraints whose scopes are not visible in any one context. Relation-valued local data introduce a different obstruction: pairwise-consistent local relations need not admit a global relation when the context hypergraph is cyclic. This paper models a context as a finite typed atom set with definedness-sensitive partial sections and canonical restrictions. It keeps label coverage, relation-coordinate coverage, type and convention guards, and overlap compatibility as separate conditions. For a declared global constraint package, the visible package contains exactly those constraints whose complete scopes occur in at least one local context. title: Dynamic Neural Topology Graph Learning (DNTGL)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Neural Topology Graph Learning (DNTGL), a novel approach to neural network training that leverages the principles of self-organization found in biological neural networks. DNTGL departs from traditional methods that rely on pre-defined, static network topologies, instead dynamically adapting and optimizing network structure through a probabilistic mechanism of neuronal connection growth and shrinkage. The core of DNTGL lies in the concept of 'local perception' where neurons assess their connections based on the topology of their immediate neighborhood and learned association strengths. This dynamic interaction, coupled with a topology entropy objective function, allows the network to evolve a topology specifically tailored to the input data, overcoming the limitations of fixed topology architectures. The key contribution of this work is the integration of dynamic topology learning with association strength learning, offering a framework capable of handling highly complex and uncertain network structures. We demonstrate, theoretically, the potential of DNTGL to surpass conventional neural network training methods in scenarios demanding adaptability and optimization of network topology. ---
