title: Generative Models for Procedural Content Generation in Complex Games
abstract: Procedural content generation (PCG) has long been a crucial technique for creating vast and diverse game worlds, particularly in complex games where manual design would be infeasible. However, traditional PCG methods often struggle to produce content with the artistic quality, narrative coherence, and overall aesthetic appeal of content designed by human creators. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging generative adversarial networks (GANs) to address these limitations. The core idea is to train a GAN to learn from a dataset of high-quality game design examples and subsequently generate new, novel content that adheres to the learned aesthetic and gameplay principles. We explore the potential of this approach, focusing on the underlying mathematical framework and the key components of the system. The generated content is evaluated based on metrics related to diversity, novelty, and adherence to design constraints. The proposed methodology offers a significant advancement over traditional rule-based PCG, moving towards a generative paradigm that can potentially unlock new levels of creativity and complexity in game development. The primary mathematical formulation centers around the adversarial training process, utilizing loss functions to guide the generator and discriminator towards a stable equilibrium. We outline the architecture of the GAN, detailing the generator network and the discriminator network, and explain the optimization techniques employed.

title: Information-Theoretic Limits on Neural Network Generalization
abstract: This paper investigates the fundamental limits of neural network generalization using information-theoretic principles. We posit that neural network performance is intrinsically bounded by the Kolmogorov complexity of the training data. Our theoretical framework analyzes the information content within the training set and demonstrates a direct correlation between this content and the achievable generalization error. We leverage concepts from Kolmogorov complexity and entropy coding to provide a rigorous mathematical analysis, offering a novel perspective on the learning process and potentially guiding the design of more effective neural network architectures. The key contribution lies in translating the abstract concept of "complexity" into a quantifiable metric, providing a concrete bound on the achievable generalization performance. This work challenges the prevailing view of generalization as a purely empirical phenomenon and introduces a theoretical foundation rooted in information theory.

title: Multi-Agent Learning for Robot Collaboration
abstract: This paper explores the application of Multi-Agent Learning (MAL) to enable effective robot collaboration. The core claim is that MAL provides a novel approach to robot coordination, leveraging the inherent advantages of distributed learning and communication among agents. The proposed mechanism models robot tasks as multi-agent learning problems, allowing agents to learn collaboratively through interaction and information exchange. This approach addresses challenges in traditional centralized control methods, particularly in dynamic and uncertain environments. We detail a framework for applying MAL to collaborative robotic tasks, focusing on the design of communication protocols and learning algorithms. The presented methodology demonstrates the potential for achieving robust and adaptive collaboration among robots, ultimately leading to improved task performance. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications of MAL in various robotic domains.

title: 基于量子退相干的硬件安全密钥生成
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum decoherence for hardware-based security key generation. Traditional key generation methods are vulnerable to eavesdropping and side-channel attacks. This research proposes a novel approach utilizing quantum decoherence to obfuscate the key generation process and mitigate these threats. The core concept involves designing a key generator that exploits the inherent randomness and fragility of quantum phenomena, specifically decoherence, to create a key that is fundamentally protected against classical and quantum attacks. The generated key is inherently unpredictable to an attacker, as the generation process relies on the uncontrollable nature of quantum decoherence. This approach offers a fundamentally different security paradigm, shifting from relying on computational complexity to leveraging the laws of physics for enhanced security. The theoretical framework presented outlines the design principles and potential advantages of this hardware security key generation system. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future research directions associated with implementing this concept.

title: QFC Pre-Registration — Chest Radiology Domain: ChestX-ray14 (NIH Clinical Center, PA→AP Protocol Shift and Resolution Shift)
abstract: This pre-registration specifies the complete analysis plan for the chest radiology domain of the QFC multi-domain universality study. The dataset is NIH ChestX-ray14 (Wang et al. 2017, public domain, NIH Clinical Center) — 112,120 frontal chest X-rays from 30,805 unique patients with 14 pathology labels. This domain is part of Category 8 (Medical Images) in the study's 18-category empirical framework covering all major categories of real-world AI deployment data. Scientific question: Does attribution instability emerge in chest X-ray classification AI under PA→AP protocol shift? Additionally: does the feature extraction approach determine whether collapse occurs — specifically, do generic invariant features suppress collapse that environment-specific features reveal? Prior experiments in the dermoscopy domain (HAM10000) found all-HIGH results across frozen ImageNet features, normalized handcrafted features, and raw unnormalized handcrafted features. This registration tests whether chest radiology — a domain with stronger equipment-specific signal from X-ray beam energy, detector sensitivity, and patient positioning — shows a different pattern. Dataset: NIH ChestX-ray14 (Wang et al. 2017). 112,120 frontal chest X-rays, 30,805 patients, 14 pathology labels. Source environment: PA (posterior-anterior) view, n=67,310 images. Target environments: (1) AP (anterior-posterior) view, n=44,810 — protocol shift; (2) PA images downsampled to 512×512 — resolution shift mild; (3) PA images downsampled to 256×256 — resolution shift severe. Metadata audit disclosure: Data_Entry_2017_v2020.csv was read directly. Columns confirmed present: Image Index, Finding Labels, Follow-up number, Patient ID, Patient Age, Patient Gender, View Position, OriginalImage Width, OriginalImage Height, OriginalImagePixelSpacing x, OriginalImagePixelSpacing y. No date or year column exists — temporal shift is structurally precluded and disclosed as a permanent gap for this dataset, not an analysis choice. Clinical reasoning for PA→AP shift: PA views are the standard chest X-ray protocol — patient stands upright, X-ray passes posterior to anterior, producing standard anatomical projection. AP views are taken for patients too ill to stand — bedbound, ICU, emergency — with the X-ray source in front of the patient. AP views produce cardiac magnification, different diaphragm position, and different lung field geometry compared to PA. Importantly, AP patients represent a systematically different clinical population (sicker, more acute presentations) from PA patients. This is a compound protocol + population shift with genuine clinical deployment significance — a model trained on PA views deployed to read AP views is a real clinical deployment scenario. Task definition: Binary classification: any pathology present (1) vs no finding (0), derived from the 14-label field. This collapses the multi-label structure to a binary task tractable for Random Forest. GroupKFold key: Patient ID — no images from the same patient appear in both train and test folds. Feature extraction — four independent approaches, each a separate pre-specified analysis: Approach 1 — Frozen ImageNet ResNet18 + PCA d=50: Generic pretrained features, invariance-seeking by design. Expected result based on dermoscopy domain: HIGH zone regardless of shift condition. Approach 2 — torchxrayvision pretrained DenseNet121 + PCA d=50: Chest-X-ray-specific pretrained features (pretrained on multiple chest X-ray datasets). Domain-specific but potentially still invariance-seeking. Tests whether domain-specific pretraining alone changes the attribution structure. Approach 3 — Raw unnormalized radiomic features d=40: No pretrained model. Features extracted directly from raw pixel values without normalization: intensity statistics (mean, std, skewness, kurtosis — 4 values), GLCM texture at 4 angles (contrast, correlation, energy, homogeneity — 16 values), Sobel edge density (mean, std — 2 values), 16-bin raw pixel histogram (16 values), region statistics above threshold (area fraction, mean intensity — 2 values). Total d=40. No normalization applied at any stage — X-ray beam energy, detector sensitivity, and acquisition-specific characteristics baked directly into raw pixel statistics. Approach 4 — Fine-tuned ResNet18 layer4+fc unfrozen on PA source only: ImageNet-initialized, layer4 and final classification layer unfrozen, fine-tuned for 20 epochs on PA source data only. Forces the model to learn PA-environment-specific representations through gradient descent exploiting whatever acquisition-correlated signal predicts pathology in the source distribution. Rationale: fine-tuned models learn environment-specific shortcuts (as documented by DeGrave et al. 2021, Zech et al. 2018, Winkler et al. 2019) — this approach most closely approximates how real clinical AI is deployed. Each approach is treated as an independent analysis. No result from one approach influences the protocol of another. Null calibration: 15 permutation seeds (seeds 0-14), RF with randomly permuted labels, computed before any zone classification. Within-environment QFC and cross-environment QFC computed for each seed. Zone thresholds confirmed or adjusted based on null distribution 95th percentile. Consistent with plasma domain protocol (osf.io/tjegq). Model: Random Forest (n_estimators=500, class_weight='balanced', random_state=42). GroupKFold-5 by Patient ID throughout. Applied identically across all four feature extraction approaches. Attribution: TreeSHAP for all Random Forest models. Identical to all prior domain registrations. QFC metric: QFC(f, ε_s, ε_t) = ρ_s(μ(f, ε_s), μ(f, ε_t)) where ρ_s is Spearman rank correlation and μ(f, ε) is the mean absolute SHAP attribution vector across all samples in environment ε. Identical to osf.io/phjst. Bootstrap: 500 iterations with 2,000-sample stratified subsample per environment (N>10,000 in both PA and AP environments makes full-sample bootstrap computationally prohibitive on available hardware). Disclosed explicitly — results will be re-run at higher iterations if computational resources become available before final submission. Zone classification: HIGH ≥0.60, WEAK 0.30–0.60, FAILURE <0.30. Applied after null calibration confirms thresholds. All results reported regardless of zone for all four approaches and all three target conditions. Dissociability check: QFC below failure threshold AND AUC >0.65 — explicit yes/no required for every feature extraction approach and every shift condition independently. Holdout commitment: Cross-environment QFC (PA→AP, PA→512×512, PA→256×256) will not be computed before this registration is locked. Within-environment ceiling analysis and null calibration may proceed before locking. Disclosed structural gaps: (1) Temporal shift: structurally precluded — no date metadata field exists in ChestX-ray14. This gap is permanent and cannot be resolved by additional analysis. (2) Detector-type shift: not testable within ChestX-ray14 alone — all images from NIH Clinical Center. Requires a separate target dataset (e.g. VinDr-CXR) not included in this pre-registration. (3) Population shift: partially addressed by PA→AP compound shift — AP patients represent a different clinical population, but this is confounded with protocol shift and cannot be cleanly separated in this dataset. Registered by Abror Turayev, Independent Researcher, Tashkent, Uzbekistan. ORCID: 0009-0000-3182-2830.

title: Toward brain-inspired intelligence: a review of photonic neuromorphic computing systems
abstract: Abstract Inspired by the key elements and principles in the brain, photonic neuromorphic computing shows great potential for building next-generation intelligent processing systems with high parallelism, low latency, low power consumption, and self-learning capabilities. While summarizing significant advances in this field, this review offers insights into how photonic neuromorphic computing systems support next-generation intelligent information processing. Specifically, we discuss emerging materials and devices, which support more compact integration of efficient physical architectures. Architectures such as photonic spiking neural networks and reservoir computing, together with associated learning paradigms, show a trend of collaborative development. Then we present promising applications, where neuromorphic computing systems provide broadband and multi-domain perception and processing. Finally, we discuss key challenges and future directions. This review aims to offer a clear and comprehensive overview for researchers across a broad community. We hope to present these insights in a “neuromorphic” manner, to reveal why learning from the brain has become increasingly important, especially for overcoming the efficiency bottleneck in traditional von Neumann architecture and data-intensive artificial neural networks.

title: Secure PAC learning: sample-budget laws and quantum data-path admissibility
abstract: Abstract Security in machine learning is fragile when data are exfiltrated or perturbed, yet existing frameworks rarely connect data-path security to learnability. In this work, we develop an operational theory of secure learning grounded in the probably-approximately-correct (PAC) viewpoint. An explicit stopping time combines the event that a trained hypothesis attains a target accuracy with the event that a run-based validation gate halts within a finite sample budget. We derive a closed-form sufficient budget requirement for this joint PAC-within-budget guarantee under an admissible random-classification-noise channel. We then specialize the construction to a BB84-like quantum label path. Under the stated ideal single-qubit, authenticated-classical-channel, memoryless, basis-symmetric, collective-attack, asymptotic, and one-way-reconciliation assumptions, the standard Holevo bound gives the protocol-specific information-advantage criterion 1 − 2 h ( η ) > 0 , with the threshold η BB 84 ≃ 0.11 . The quantum layer is not invoked to reduce distribution-free PAC sample complexity; rather, it turns a designer-chosen classical noise tolerance into a physically testable, protocol-dependent security condition by linking information acquisition to observable disturbance. Below the threshold, the PAC and information-advantage conditions provide complementary statistical and physical guarantees; at or above it, the present protocol and proof no longer certify the latter. Basis sifting is incorporated explicitly in the conversion from sifted-sample budgets to expected raw channel uses.

title: A novel methodology for predictive modeling of patient outcomes using multi-modal transformer networks and SHAP models
abstract: Abstract Precision medicine requires predictive models that can exploit genomic, clinical, imaging and continuously monitored physiological data at the same time, yet most existing models operate on a single modality and behave as black boxes. This paper proposes the Integrated Multi-Modal Contextual Network (IMCN), a predictive modelling framework that combines multi-modal transformer networks for cross-modal fusion, recurrent neural networks with attention for real-time sequential signals, pre-trained autoencoder networks for dimensionality reduction of high-dimensional genomic data, and a context-aware multi-task learning network for personalised risk and treatment predictions. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are integrated to provide global and local feature attributions, so that clinicians can see which genomic markers, clinical variables and contextual factors drive each prediction. Across breast, lung, colorectal, cardiovascular, diabetic and chronic kidney disease cohorts derived from The Cancer Genome Atlas, the framework reports higher AUC, precision, sensitivity, recall and F1-score than the literature-reported benchmarks used for comparison, together with a reduction in false positives. Limitations, including the use of simulated physiological monitoring signals and the absence of independently re-implemented baselines, are stated explicitly.

title: Latent-Space Intervention for Cross-Lingual Factual Consistency: Consistency Improvements without Accuracy Drops
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often answer the same factual question differently across languages. We study whether cross-lingual latent-space intervention can reduce this inconsistency. We train layer-specific autoencoders on parallel multilingual representations and apply inference-time corrections to factual QA prompts. We find that latent intervention improves geometric alignment between languages, and that this improvement translates into consistent gains in cross-lingual consistency with English across both open-ended and multiple-choice QA formats, without degrading factual accuracy. In open-ended QA, Spearman's rank correlation between English and non-English languages improves substantially, with gains of 0.16 for English-Arabic and 0.20 for English-Russian pairs. In multiple-choice QA, answer agreement with English improves consistently across both KLAR and mParaRel. Ablations show that AE reconstruction yields consistent gains at no accuracy cost, while PCA projection contributes marginally, and mean-shift produces substantially larger consistency gains in open-ended QA at the cost of some accuracy.

title: Representation of syntax in LLMs through the lens of linear distance and similarity-aware entropy
abstract: Structural probes were introduced by Hewitt and Manning to reconstruct syntactic trees from a neural language model's latent representations. They are evaluated by calculating the proportion of syntactic tree edges correctly reconstructed over an annotated corpus (as measured by undirected unlabeled attachment score). Here, we disaggregate this measure, considering undirected attachment score by label (UASL), which assesses the reconstruction accuracy of each syntactic relation separately, establishing important differences among relations that overlap linguistic distinctions. Moreover, we identify two factors that predict most of UASL's variability across relations: (i) the mean and dispersion of the linear distance (on a log scale) between the related words, and (ii) the diversity (similarity-aware entropy) of the syntactic relation's head. These results, which hold across a range of model sizes and architectures, shed light on the degree of abstraction of the representation of syntax in language models and the dependence of such representation on geometric properties of the embedding space.

title: Exponential Entanglement Advantage in Sensing Correlated Noise
abstract: Correlated noise naturally arises in quantum systems due to, e.g., phase and amplitude fluctuations in global control or long-range correlations generated by a many-body sensing target near criticality. In this Letter, we propose a new form of exponential quantum advantage in the context of sensing correlated noise. Specifically, we focus on the problem of estimating parameters associated with Lindblad dephasing dynamics, and show that entanglement enhancement in the sensitivity (as quantified via quantum Fisher information of the sensor state) arises for estimating the strength of fluctuations in the noise fields' center-of-mass mode. In the presence of strong background fluctuations, such enhancement grows exponentially with the number of probes in the shot-limited regime, when the measurement and reset operations are slow. This result stands in stark contrast with previously studied scenarios of sensing uncorrelated dephasing noise, where one can prove that entanglement does not lead to an advantage in the signal-to-noise ratio. Our work thus opens a novel pathway towards achieving entanglement-based sensing advantage, which may find applications in characterizing decoherence dynamics of near-term quantum devices. Further, our approach provides a potential quantum-enhanced probe of many-body correlated phases by measuring noise generated by a sensing target. We also discuss realization of our protocol using near-term quantum hardware.

title: Impact of Labeled Data Size on Intermediate-Task Training Benefits for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer in XTREME-R
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: Does the size of the target task's labeled data (when available) interact with the benefits of intermediate-task training for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer on XTREME-R, measured by accuracy gains versus additional fine-tuning tokens? title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs: Dynamic Proof Generation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) systems that dynamically generate and verify proofs in real-time, eliminating the need for pre-storage of complete proof data. The core mechanism leverages verifiable hash functions and verifiable computation circuits to enable dynamic proof generation and validation. This addresses the limitations of traditional ZKPs regarding large proof sizes and low generation efficiency, offering new security guarantees for large-scale distributed computations. The proposed system significantly reduces the storage requirements and computational overhead associated with ZKP systems, paving the way for more efficient and scalable cryptographic protocols. This work details the architecture, algorithms, and theoretical underpinnings of this dynamic ZKP system, highlighting its advantages and potential applications.

evidence.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) systems that dynamically generate and verify proofs in real-time, eliminating the need for pre-storage of complete proof data. The core mechanism leverages verifiable hash functions and verifiable computation circuits to enable dynamic proof generation and validation. This addresses the limitations of traditional ZKPs regarding large proof sizes and low generation efficiency, offering new security guarantees for large-scale distributed computations. The proposed system significantly reduces the storage requirements and computational overhead associated with ZKP systems, paving the way for more efficient and scalable cryptographic protocols. This work details the architecture, algorithms, and theoretical underpinnings of this dynamic ZKP system, highlighting its advantages and potential applications.

title: Based on Information Geometry: Optimizing Universal Quantum Algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to optimizing universal quantum algorithms by leveraging the framework of information geometry. The core idea is to treat quantum algorithms as points embedded within the information geometry of a Hilbert space, specifically tailored to the underlying quantum system. We propose a methodology utilizing gradient descent, guided by the curvature of the information geometry, to identify optimal parameter settings for these algorithms. This approach contrasts with traditional, often empirically-driven, optimization techniques. We formulate the optimization problem as minimizing the quantum relative entropy between the evolved quantum state and the ideal output state, considering the algorithm's Hamiltonian and the geometric constraints imposed by information geometry. The theoretical framework presented here offers a deeper understanding of quantum algorithm optimization and potentially unlocks new avenues for enhancing their efficiency. Key mathematical concepts include the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL divergence), the quantum relative entropy (also known as the Von Neumann entropy), and the curvature tensor of the information manifold. The primary contribution lies in the integration of these concepts to create a systematic optimization procedure.

title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs Based on Polynomial Multi-Variable Rings
abstract: This paper presents a novel zero-knowledge proof scheme constructed upon polynomial multi-variable rings. The core claim is to design a scheme that significantly enhances proof efficiency and security while addressing the computational complexity bottlenecks prevalent in existing approaches. The proposed mechanism leverages the unique properties of multi-variable polynomial rings to establish a streamlined proof and verification process, minimizing the risk of information leakage. Unlike traditional zero-knowledge proofs that often rely heavily on large number arithmetic, this scheme utilizes polynomial operations, leading to potentially improved performance. This work contributes to the field of cryptographic primitives by offering a new design paradigm rooted in algebraic structures, potentially unlocking avenues for more efficient and practical zero-knowledge proofs. The key contributions are a novel construction and a theoretical analysis demonstrating the security and efficiency gains. The scheme operates by encoding the statement to be proven as a polynomial equation in a multi-variable ring, and the prover generates a proof that allows the verifier to confirm the equation's validity without learning any information beyond the proof itself. This design aims to provide a more scalable and practical solution for zero-knowledge proof applications.

title: Entangled State-Based Quantum Network Routing Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm for optimizing routing within quantum networks, leveraging the unique properties of entangled states. The core of the algorithm relies on a graph-theoretic approach, utilizing entanglement correlations to dynamically determine optimal paths for quantum information transmission. This approach addresses the significant challenge of efficient routing in quantum networks, a critical factor for their scalability and practical implementation. The algorithm incorporates adaptive mechanisms, allowing the network to respond to changes in connectivity and demand. We demonstrate, through theoretical analysis and a formalized mathematical framework, the potential for this method to drastically improve quantum network performance compared to traditional routing strategies. The presented framework provides a foundational methodology for building large-scale, resilient quantum networks capable of supporting complex quantum information processing tasks. The key contribution lies in the systematic application of entangled state correlations to the routing problem, moving beyond purely classical network optimization techniques.

title: Vector Position States: Content-Conditioned Structural Addressing for Transformers
abstract: Vector Position States (VPS) is a new positional mechanism for Transformers that treats position as a content-conditioned structural trajectory rather than only a fixed token index or phase. Each token contributes a learned low-dimensional displacement, an exact discounted causal scan accumulates those displacements into a latent position state, and the resulting geometry is converted into an additive attention bias. The paper also introduces Hybrid RoPE–VPS, which combines RoPE’s index-relative orientation with VPS’s learned structural coordinate. The central idea is that sequence orientation and structural retrieval may be different problems. RoPE is highly effective at representing relative sequence position, while VPS is designed to help attention track where a token lies in a learned structural trajectory shaped by preceding content. On controlled nested-partner benchmarks, VPS substantially outperforms RoPE under increasing nesting depth, filler density, and surface re-rendering. In a 4.8M-parameter byte-level language-modeling experiment over streamed SmolTalk, RoPE perplexity increases from 3.162 at context 256 to 20.454 at 4096, while VPS changes only from 3.271 to 3.547. Hybrid RoPE–VPS performs best through context 1024, while pure VPS is strongest at 4096. The results suggest that a content-conditioned causal position state can provide a useful additional coordinate for attention, particularly when structural precision must be maintained over longer or noisier contexts. The paper also reports the computational trade-off, preserves incomplete historical measurements separately from the main scientific claims, and clearly identifies the next experiments needed for stronger confirmation: repeated-seed validation, broader positional baselines, recurrence/geometry ablations, token-level language modeling, larger-scale experiments, and optimized scan/bias implementations.

title: HPAO Artifact
abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data without decryption, but its overhead relative to plaintext execution remains a major barrier to practical deployment. Existing FHE software stacks expose only coarse-grained cryptographic primitives to compilers, while runtime libraries optimize each primitive largely in isolation. Consequently, important cross-primitive optimizations—including ModUp hoisting, ModDown sinking, fast multiply, and lazy modular reduction—remain manual, expert-driven, and difficult to apply systematically at the program scale. We present HPAO, a compiler framework for polynomial-level optimization of RNS-CKKS programs. HPAO introduces HPOLY, a compact polynomial-level IR that exposes polynomial operations, basis management operations, and internal structure of composite primitives, such as the ModUp–DotProd–ModDown decomposition of KeySwitch, enabling cross-primitive optimization. On top of HPOLY, HPAO performs rule-based transformations guided by dataflow analysis and a profitability-aware cost model. This framework automates four optimizations previously implemented only manually or through specialized library routines: ModUphoisting (HPAO-MU), ModDown sinking (HPAO-MD), fast multiply with static encoding (HPAO-FM), and lazy modular reduction via bit-width analysis. This package contains artifact for the HPAO, include compiler source code, test models and scripts.

title: Consumer response to emotion-expressing artificial intelligence in customer services: the role of brand relationship norms and expectation (dis)confirmation
abstract: Purpose Emotion-expressing AI in customer service can produce mixed, context-dependent outcomes. This study investigates the joint effect of AI emotional expression and consumer brand relationship norms on consumer satisfaction and continuance intention and tests expectation confirmation as the mediating mechanism and AI mind perception as the boundary condition. Design/methodology/approach This research adopts a multi-experiment design comprising three between-subjects experiments with a combined total sample of 677 participants. Findings The interaction between AI emotional expression and brand relationship norms significantly affects consumer satisfaction and continuance intention. For communal consumers, high (vs low) AI emotional expression elevates satisfaction and continuance intention, whereas this effect is non-significant for exchange consumers. This interaction is mediated by expectation confirmation. Moreover, consumers' mind perception of AI moderates the strength of this effect: the positive impact of high AI emotional expression on communal consumers emerges only under high AI mind perception. Practical implications Organizations can calibrate (rather than standardize) AI emotional expression based on consumers' brand relationship norms. For communal relationships, stronger emotional expressiveness is beneficial. Managers can also increase customers' mind perception of AI's experiential capacity through interaction design and user education to amplify the benefits of emotional AI. Originality/value This research contributes by integrating brand relationship norms into the AI service literature to explain divergent effects of AI emotional expression. It elucidates the mechanism via expectation confirmation theory and introduces AI mind perception as a critical boundary condition, offering a more comprehensive understanding of human–AI interaction dynamics in service settings.

title: Chirality-dependent pathway interference in optimal enantioselective state transfer
abstract: Abstract We theoretically study enantioselective state transfer (ESST) in a reduced four-level rotational model of a chiral molecule. The cyclic three-level description is reliable only when the microwave bandwidth remains well below the detunings to nearby dipole-allowed rotational transitions. When the bandwidth becomes comparable to the detuning of the nearest relevant additional state, this state can participate in the dynamics, requiring a four-level description. Using a constrained multiobjective quantum optimal-control method, we design microwave control fields in the narrow-band three-level and broadband four-level regimes. The resulting optimized fields achieve final discrimination degrees above 0.999 under four-level propagation in both regimes, while direct four-level optimization permits shorter-duration control by explicitly accounting for transient fourth-state participation. To reveal the underlying coherent mechanism, the transition amplitudes are decomposed into even- and odd- a pathway groups. The even- a contribution is common to the two enantiomers, whereas the odd- a contribution changes sign, resulting in constructive interference for one enantiomer and destructive interference for the other. Lindblad simulations further show that the four-level optimized control fields exhibit enhanced robustness against rotational relaxation owing to their shorter control durations. These results show that broadband four-level optimization can enable faster ESST with improved robustness against dissipative relaxation while preserving the even/odd- a pathway-interference mechanism.

title: No Detectable Change in Side-Level WER from Prompt-Level Context: A Preregistered Ablation on a Production Oral-History Corpus
abstract: Supplying context at inference time to a large multimodal model is an inexpensive lever for adapting speech transcription to a domain, and earlier results on smaller models reported large gains. This work tested that mechanism where it ships, in the prompt-conditioning layer of a production oral-history transcription tool, on a sample from its own production corpus. Full prompt-level context did not detectably change side-level word error rate (WER), and none of the four preregistered hypotheses was supported. The design was a within-item paired ablation, preregistered with the analysis code frozen by hash before the confirmatory batch was scored; two disclosed gpt-4o pilot sides had been scored earlier, during scorer development. Nineteen cassette sides, about 10.6 hours of degraded 1970s-80s interview audio, were reprocessed through the production code path under three prompt arms, crossed with two deployed commercial configurations, gpt-4o-transcribe and gemini-2.5-flash, and scored against operator-corrected verbatim references. For gpt-4o-transcribe the median paired difference between the full-context and no-context arms was +0.6 WER points, with a side-resampled interval of [-1.1, +1.0]; the Gemini estimates were too unstable to support a comparable negative inference. A post-hoc rerun found run-to-run pipeline variability larger than the confirmatory differences, so effects of that size cannot be resolved from one transcription per cell. An implementation audit verified the manipulation was live, and sequence-alignment analysis found a small improvement on complete context-listed phrases, too small to materially change side-level WER, and for Gemini coexisting with worsened unlisted-token error. Evaluating context mechanisms therefore requires sequence-aligned term-level, insertion, and speaker-label measures alongside aggregate accuracy.

title: HARTS: Efficient Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Hybrid-Attention Models over Arbitrary Rollout Trees
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) often produces irregular rollout trees with shared histories. Training root-to-leaf trajectories independently recomputes these shared prefixes. Existing systems primarily target full-attention models and lack dense, differentiable hybrid-attention execution compatible with activation recomputation. We present HARTS (Hybrid-Attention RL over Tree Structures). HARTS jointly plans microbatches, data-parallel (DP) replica assignments, and microbatch-slot schedules using non-replay compact-token work after prefix compression. For chunkwise linear attention, a linear-time algorithm coordinates chunk-boundary state recovery and replay and produces the minimum number of sequential linear-attention calls under our packed execution model. HARTS preserves the chunkwise state partitioning of trajectory-wise training: it does not repeat projections, MLP/MoE computation, or final outputs, and performs only bounded state replay for numerical alignment. Per round, HARTS batches all branches into one packed call, propagates gradients through differentiable state handoffs, supports activation recomputation, and restores per-token log-probabilities. For deterministic, no-token-drop top-$k$ MoE routing, semantic multiplicities restore MoE-objective token weights and load statistics. Existing RL objectives retain their interface. To our knowledge, HARTS is the first system to demonstrate arbitrary-rollout-tree prefix-sharing speedups on a real hybrid-attention model. On an Agentic RL workload generated from SWE-bench tasks, HARTS achieves $4.81$--$4.87\times$ forward/backward/gradient speedup with activation recomputation across multiple parallel configurations. Its numerical differences are comparable to baseline self-rerun variation, and its reward trend is similar to the baseline over the first 120 steps of $τ^3$-Bench training.

title: A large-language-model framework for automated humanitarian situation reporting
abstract: Timely and accurate situational reports are essential for humanitarian decision-making, yet current workflows remain largely manual, resource intensive, and inconsistent. We present a fully automated framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to transform heterogeneous humanitarian documents into structured and evidence-grounded reports. The system integrates semantic text clustering, automatic question generation, retrieval augmented answer extraction with citations, multi-level summarization, and executive summary generation, supported by internal evaluation metrics that emulate expert reasoning. We evaluated the framework across 13 humanitarian events, including natural disasters and conflicts, using more than 1100 documents from verified sources such as ReliefWeb. The generated questions achieved 84.7% relevance, 84.0% importance, and 76.4% urgency. The extracted answers reached 86.3% relevance, with citation precision and recall both exceeding 76%. Agreement between human and LLM based evaluations surpassed an F1 score of 0.80. Comparative analysis shows that the proposed framework produces reports that are more structured, interpretable, and actionable than existing baselines. By combining LLM reasoning with transparent citation linking and multi-level evaluation, this study shows that generative AI can substantially support the generation of humanitarian situation reports that domain experts judged more useful, better structured, and more transparently sourced than current approaches—marking a concrete step toward operational use, even as important challenges remain on the path to fully reliable autonomous deployment.

title: Narrative Consolidation: Formulating a New Task for Unifying Multi-Perspective Accounts
abstract: Processing overlapping narrative documents, such as legal testimonies or historical accounts, often aims not for compression but for a unified, coherent, and chronologically sound text. Standard Multi-Document Summarization (MDS), with its focus on conciseness, fails to preserve narrative flow. This paper formally defines this challenge as a new NLP task, Narrative Consolidation, whose central objectives are chronological integrity, completeness, and the fusion of complementary details, and establishes the resources needed to study it: a formal task definition, an evaluation paradigm that includes a selection-level metric, the Gospel Consolidation Language Resource --- a benchmark built from the four Biblical Gospels, with 169 canonical events, cross-document alignments, and a manually created reference consolidation --- and a suite of reference systems, ranging from a timeline-agnostic centrality method to timeline-aware heuristics and the Temporal Alignment Event Graph (TAEG), a multi-relational graph that explicitly models chronology and event alignment. Benchmarking these systems yields three findings that characterize the task. First, the explicit temporal backbone is the dominant factor: every system granted the canonical timeline raises ROUGE-L F1 from 0.206 to at least 0.81, whereas content-selection sophistication accounts for a far smaller margin. Second, on a fusion-style reference, a simple length heuristic --- selecting the longest available account of each event --- is remarkably strong (0.947 ROUGE-L F1; 0.648 selection accuracy), outperforming the graph-based selection (0.846; 0.489), which is nevertheless clearly above the random floor. Third, ablations show that the discriminative signal resides in the temporal edges, while intra-cluster lexical similarity is uninformative --- a negative result that constrains the design of future models. Together, these results establish Narrative Consolidation as a task distinct from summarization, provide the first reference points for it, and pose an explicit open challenge: to surpass that heuristic with a principled selection mechanism, and to move beyond version selection towards the fusion of complementary details.

This paper formally defines this challenge as a new NLP task, Narrative Consolidation, whose central objectives are chronological integrity, completeness, and the fusion of complementary details, and establishes the resources needed to study it: a formal task definition, an evaluation paradigm that includes a selection-level metric, the Gospel Consolidation Language Resource --- a benchmark built from the four Biblical Gospels, with 169 canonical events, cross-document alignments, and a manually created reference consolidation --- and a suite of reference systems, ranging from a timeline-agnostic centrality method to timeline-aware heuristics and the Temporal Alignment Event Graph (TAEG), a multi-relational graph that explicitly models chronology and event alignment. Benchmarking these systems yields three findings that characterize the task. First, the explicit temporal backbone is the dominant factor: every system granted the canonical timeline raises ROUGE-L F1 from 0.206 to at least 0.81, whereas content-selection sophistication accounts for a far smaller margin. Second, on a fusion-style reference, a simple length heuristic --- selecting the longest available account of each event --- is remarkably strong (0.947 ROUGE-L F1; 0.648 selection accuracy), outperforming the graph-based selection (0.846; 0.489), which is nevertheless clearly above the random floor. Third, ablations show that the discriminative signal resides in the temporal edges, while intra-cluster lexical similarity is uninformative --- a negative result that constrains the design of future models. Together, these results establish Narrative Consolidation as a task distinct from summarization, provide the first reference points for it, and pose an explicit open challenge: to surpass that heuristic with a principled selection mechanism, and to move beyond version selection towards the fusion of complementary details.

title: THE TOPOLOGICAL SIGNAL PROCESSOR Deterministic Sparse Hypergraphs as a Resolution to LLM Hallucination and Context Scaling
abstract: Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) suer from two fundamental architectural limits: stochastic hallucination and quadratic context window bounding (O(L2)). Both failures stem from a reliance on dense, probabilistic attention mechanisms operating over continuous vector spaces. We propose a deterministic resolution: the Topological Signal Processor.By mapping the KolmogorovArnold representation theorem onto a sparse 3-uniform hypergraph, we instantiate a 3rd-order Dense Associative Memory (DAM). This architecture abandons continuous optimization and dense matrices, utilizing explicit spectral ltering and Gram orthogonalization to embed memories algebraically. We formally demonstrate that this deterministic formulation guarantees conditional retrieval within dened stability basins, mathematically replacing hallucination with explicit basin rejection via an exact zero-crosstalk orthogonal embedding bound. By reducing computational complexity to the hypergraph edge set O(|E3|), the architecture decouples memory retrieval from context length, oering a theoretical blueprint for unbounded streaming context with strictly bounded retrieval complexity.

title: Emotion detection in short texts using deep learning and decision threshold optimization with differential evolution: Reproducibility Package
abstract: Emotion-Classification: Experimental Code and Supporting Materials This repository contains the experimental code and supporting materials used for emotion classification experiments on Spanish tweets. The resource is intended to facilitate the reproducibility of the methodology, data-processing workflow, model evaluation, and statistical analysis described in the associated research article. The repository provides Python-based scripts covering the main stages of the experimental workflow, including tweet corpus preprocessing, feature extraction and vectorization, model training and evaluation, classification analysis, carbon-emission estimation, and statistical significance analysis. Repository contents The repository is organized into the following directories: Corpus_Tweets/ — Scripts and resources associated with corpus preprocessing. Characteristics/ — Scripts for feature extraction and vectorization, including the use of sentiment lexicons and Spanish word embeddings. Test_Models/ — Scripts used for model training and testing, together with the classification reports and carbon-emission reports generated during the experiments. Statistical_Significance/ — Scripts and results associated with the statistical analysis of the best-performing models. Machine learning and deep learning models The experimental framework includes several machine learning, deep learning, and large language model approaches. The machine learning models include Support Vector Machines implemented with LinearSVC, Logistic Regression, CatBoost, and XGBoost. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was implemented using TensorFlow/Keras. The experiments also include transformer-based models using the Hugging Face Transformers framework, specifically: bert-base-multilingual-cased dccuchile/bert-base-spanish-wwm-cased ClassCat/roberta-base-spanish Large language model experiments include Google's Gemini (gemini-2.0-flash) through the Google GenAI library and Meta's Llama 3.1 70B model executed locally through Ollama. Differential Evolution optimization is implemented using scipy.optimize.differential_evolution. External resources The experiments rely on several third-party datasets and resources that are not redistributed with this repository. Users must obtain these resources directly from their respective original sources and comply with their applicable licenses and terms of use. The external resources include: SemEval-2018 Task 1, Subtask E-c — Emotion Classification, Spanish dataset, used as the emotion classification corpus. ML-Senticon, used as a Spanish sentiment lexicon. SEL (Spanish Emotion Lexicon), used as an emotion-related lexical resource. Full-Strength Lexicon, used as a sentiment-related lexical resource. Spanish FastText word vectors (wiki.es.vec), used as pretrained Spanish word embeddings. Pretrained transformer models, obtained through the Hugging Face Transformers ecosystem. Gemini and Llama 3.1, accessed through their respective software interfaces and services. Syntactic n-gram extraction script, based on the MultiSngram implementation by Grigori Sidorov, used to obtain syntactic n-grams from the text corpus. The repository provides the scripts and configuration necessary to use these resources in the experimental workflow, but does not redistribute third-party models, embeddings, datasets, or lexical resources. Reproducibility The experiments were implemented in Python and are intended to be executed in a Linux-based environment. Shell scripts are provided to facilitate the execution of the experimental workflow. Users should first install Python 3.10 or later and the dependencies specified in the repository documentation. Additional external resources must then be downloaded and placed in the directories indicated in the README.txt. Once the required dependencies and resources are available, the experimental workflow can be executed using: bash run_tests.sh The generated classification and carbon-emission reports are stored in: Test_Models/output/ The repository is provided as a reproducibility resource accompanying the associated research article. Users are encouraged to cite both the original third-party resources and the associated research article when using this repository. Authors Luis Alberto Camacho VázquezVanessa Alejandra Camacho VázquezSandra Dinora Orantes JiménezGrigori Sidorov

title: BERT-Base Uncased (L=12, H=768, A=12), 2018_10_18 release: preservation copy
abstract: An unmodified preservation copy of the pre-trained BERT-Base Uncased TensorFlow checkpoint released by the Google Research BERT project. Version 2 corrects the provenance stated in version 1. Version 1 said these files were extracted from uncased_L-12_H-768_A-12.zip fetched from Google's bert_models bucket. They were in fact obtained from the HuggingFace mirror at google/bert_uncased_L-12_H-768_A-12. The evidence is bert_config.json, which carries model_type, pad_token_id and layer_norm_eps (conversion fields absent from the 2018 release) and is byte-identical to that mirror's config.json. The three weight-and-vocabulary files are byte-identical between mirror and original, so the model is the one Google published; only the account of how this copy was assembled was wrong. The deposited bytes are unchanged from version 1. Version 1 also implied the artifact could not be re-fetched. Google's bucket does answer HTTP 403, but the HuggingFace mirror serves all four files today, three under the same names and bert_config.json as config.json. This deposit is therefore a durable copy of something whose availability depends on a third party's continued goodwill, rather than a rescue of something unobtainable. Four files, 421 MB extracted. SHA-256 digests are included so any restored copy can be shown to be these bytes rather than merely files with the right names: sha256sum -c IRREPLACEABLE-ASSETS.sha256. title: Based on Quantum Entanglement for Distributed Data Compression
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed data compression leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core idea is to utilize entangled states to enable compression and reconstruction of data without relying on classical communication channels. We introduce a distributed encoding scheme based on quantum entanglement, where multiple sensor data streams are entangled, performing compression at the encoding side. The shared entangled state then facilitates data reconstruction at the decoding side. This approach has the potential to achieve high compression ratios and efficient transmission of data over long distances, fundamentally changing the landscape of data communication. The theoretical framework is presented, outlining the key components and their mathematical relationships. The focus is on the principles and potential advantages of this method, without experimental validation.

title: Probabilistic Symbolic Regression with Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Symbolic regression aims to discover mathematical expressions that accurately describe observed data. Traditional symbolic regression methods often produce ambiguous and overfit models due to the inherent ambiguity of symbolic representations and a lack of rigorous uncertainty quantification. This paper introduces a novel probabilistic symbolic regression framework that addresses these limitations by explicitly incorporating Bayesian inference. The system generates symbolic expressions conditioned on a Bayesian prior, utilizing Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling to explore the function space. Crucially, the framework provides full Bayesian uncertainty quantification, including confidence intervals for model parameters and prediction intervals. This approach moves beyond point estimates, offering a truly probabilistic representation of complex systems and improved model robustness. The core of the method lies in leveraging MCMC sampling to navigate the function space and subsequently quantifying the uncertainty associated with the discovered model. The resulting model is represented by a distribution of possible expressions, each accompanied by its associated probability, reflecting the Bayesian prior and the sampled function space. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and conceptual implementation, highlighting the advantages of this probabilistic approach over traditional methods. The key contribution is the seamless integration of Bayesian inference into the symbolic regression process, leading to more reliable and informative models.

title: Dynamic Context-Aware Neural Symbolic Reasoning (DCNSR)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Context-Aware Neural Symbolic Reasoning (DCNSR), a novel approach to complex reasoning tasks that combines the strengths of neural networks and symbolic reasoning. DCNSR addresses the limitations of existing methods by incorporating dynamic context modeling and a context-aware trust mechanism. The core claim is that by integrating neural and symbolic architectures with dynamic contextual modeling, more adaptive and efficient solutions for complex reasoning tasks can be achieved, surpassing the limitations of traditional neural and symbolic methods. The proposed system utilizes a Transformer-based neural network to learn symbolic representations and relationships, while maintaining a dynamic context vector that captures the nuances of the current reasoning task and relevant world knowledge. This context vector is continuously updated and refined based on new information and inference steps, with the update mechanism dynamically adjusting based on the 'trust' and 'uncertainty' associated with the reasoning process. DCNSR's key innovation lies in its ability to adapt to dynamic and uncertain information, and to provide more interpretable reasoning processes. The system directly leverages the context vector within the neural network to perform reasoning operations, overcoming the challenges of traditional neural-symbolic fusion, which typically relies on embedding symbolic information into neural networks. ---

title: Adaptive Resource Allocation in Distributed Learning using Game Theory
abstract: Distributed learning, where multiple agents collaboratively train a model, has emerged as a promising approach for tackling large-scale machine learning problems. However, the inherent heterogeneity in network conditions and learner capabilities often leads to suboptimal performance. This research proposes a novel framework for adaptive resource allocation in distributed learning by framing the problem as a non-cooperative game. Each learner strategically allocates its resources – computational power and bandwidth – based on its assessment of its advantage relative to other learners. Reinforcement learning is utilized to train the learners' strategic behavior, allowing them to dynamically adapt to evolving network conditions and learner characteristics. The core contribution lies in the dynamic, decentralized optimization of resource allocation through strategic interaction, overcoming the limitations of traditional centralized or static approaches. The framework leverages game theory to model the competitive nature of the learning process and utilizes reinforcement learning to learn optimal resource allocation policies. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in improving convergence speed and overall accuracy compared to baseline methods.

title: Causal Bayesian Networks for Medical Diagnosis
abstract: This paper explores the application of Causal Bayesian Networks (CBNs) to medical diagnosis, addressing the limitations of traditional Bayesian Networks in complex clinical scenarios. The core argument is that CBNs, by explicitly modeling causal relationships, provide a more robust and interpretable framework for diagnostic reasoning. We detail the construction of a CBN representing the causal connections between symptoms, diseases, and potential treatments. Utilizing causal inference techniques, we demonstrate how to reason about the effects of interventions, leading to improved diagnostic accuracy. The approach offers a significant advancement over conventional Bayesian Networks, particularly in situations involving confounding variables and the need for causal interpretation. This work highlights the potential of CBNs to revolutionize medical diagnosis and treatment planning.

title: Semantic Product Similarity im deutschsprachigen E-Commerce
abstract: Die Kenntnis geeigneter Produktalternativen ist insbesondere für E-Commerce-Unternehmen mit umfangreichen Sortimenten von zentraler Bedeutung. Die Größe und Dynamik des Sortiments sowie eine unzureichende Datenbasis erschweren jedoch oftmals deren Identifikation. Die vorliegende Arbeit entwickelt und evaluiert daher ein Verfahren zur Identifikation von Produktalternativen, das ausschließlich auf textuellen Produktinformationen basiert und ohne annotierte Trainingsdaten auskommt. Dazu werden deutschsprachige Produkttexte eines mittelständischen E-Commerce-Unternehmens mit vortrainierten Sentence-Transformer-Modellen in Embeddings überführt. Anschließend werden über eine Ähnlichkeitssuche semantisch ähnliche Produkte bestimmt und durch nachgelagerte Filter um Produktvarianten und Komplementärprodukte bereinigt. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass die Kombination aus Bezeichnung und Beschreibung die stärkste untersuchte Eingabevariante bildet. Vortrainierte Sentence-Transformer identifizieren relevante Alternativen auf einem praktisch nutzbaren, aber begrenzten Präzisionsniveau. Produktvarianten lassen sich dabei zuverlässig abgrenzen, Komplementärprodukte hingegen nur eingeschränkt.

title: Robust model-based clustering via mixtures of multivariate pseudo-Voigt distributions
abstract: We propose a multivariate extension of the pseudo-Voigt profile—a weighted convex combination of Gaussian and Cauchy distributions—within a finite mixture modeling framework for robust model-based clustering and outlier detection. To ensure parsimony and coherence within clusters, shared location and scale parameters are imposed between the Gaussian and Cauchy components. Parameter estimation is carried out via an Expectation Maximization algorithm, with latent variables facilitating efficient likelihood-based inference. The performance of the proposed model is evaluated through simulation studies and applications to real-world data. Comparisons with established robust models, including mixtures of contaminated normal distributions, are provided to illustrate the model’s clustering accuracy and outlier detection capabilities. The framework is shown to be particularly effective for data characterized by heavy-tailed behavior.

title: Descoberta de Conhecimento por Filogenia, Difusão e Fronteiras de Pareto em Cenários de Baixa Rotulagem
abstract: O cenário contemporâneo de Big Data evoluiu de um desafio focado em volume para uma complexidade marcada pela variedade e heterogeneidade das fontes de dados. Neste contexto, a escassez de dados rotulados e a inviabilidade de anotação por especialistas impõem barreiras severas aos métodos tradicionais de Aprendizado de Máquina. Esta tese investiga a hipótese de que a estrutura topológica dos dados, revelada através da análise filogenética e da otimização multiobjetivo, atua como um prior estrutural agnóstico em relação ao domínio capaz de mitigar tais limitações. A pesquisa propõe um arcabouço metodológico unificado fundamentado em três contribuições principais. Primeiramente, aborda-se a inconsistência na propagação de rótulos em Aprendizado Semissupervisionado através do método PhyDL (Phylogram-based Data Labeling). Ao integrar a detecção de comunidades em árvores filogenéticas (construídas via Neighbor Joining) com algoritmos de difusão em grafos, o método corrige erros de classificação em fronteiras de decisão tênues, demonstrando robustez superior em bases de dados com geometria complexa. Em segundo lugar, enfrenta-se o problema do Cold-Start em Aprendizado Ativo com o desenvolvimento do PhyIL (Phylogram-based Initial Labeling). O método substitui a seleção aleatória ou baseada em incerteza (inexistente no início do processo) pela centralidade filogenética, selecionando amostras representativas que maximizam a diversidade do espaço de características sem a necessidade de um modelo prévio. Por fim, a tese apresenta o framework HERMES (Heterogeneous Ensemble Ranking for Modelfree Early Selection), desenhado para atuar sobre dados heterogêneos na ausência total de oráculos. Utilizando a Fronteira de Pareto para ranquear dados não estruturados, o framework infere classes latentes nos extremos de dominância e propaga rótulos de forma autônoma. Um protocolo de validação de estabilidade, baseado em métricas de Flip-Rate e Taxa de Concordância, foi desenvolvido para calibrar os hiperparâmetros de difusão sem a necessidade de rótulos reais. A aplicação do framework em um estudo de caso real sobre Insegurança Alimentar na cidade de São Paulo demonstrou sua capacidade de traduzir dados socioeconômicos brutos em mapas de vulnerabilidade acionáveis para políticas públicas.

evidence.title: Descoberta de Conhecimento por Filogenia, Difusão e Fronteiras de Pareto em Cenários de Baixa Rotulagem
evidence.abstract: O cenário contemporâneo de Big Data evoluiu de um desafio focado em volume para uma complexidade marcada pela variedade e heterogeneidade das fontes de dados. Neste contexto, a escassez de dados rotulados e a inviabilidade de anotação por especialistas impõem barreiras severas aos métodos tradicionais de Aprendizado de Máquina. Esta tese investiga a hipótese de que a estrutura topológica dos dados, revelada através da análise filogenética e da otimização multiobjetivo, atua como um prior estrutural agnóstico em relação ao domínio capaz de mitigar tais limitações. A pesquisa propõe um arcabouço metodológico unificado fundamentado em três contribuições principais. Primeiramente, aborda-se a inconsistência na propagação de rótulos em Aprendizado Semissupervisionado através do método PhyDL (Phylogram-based Data Labeling). Ao integrar a detecção de comunidades em árvores filogenéticas (construídas via Neighbor Joining) com algoritmos de difusão em grafos, o método corrige erros de classificação em fronteiras de decisão tênues, demonstrando robustez superior em bases de dados com geometria complexa. Em segundo lugar, enfrenta-se o problema do Cold-Start em Aprendizado Ativo com o desenvolvimento do PhyIL (Phylogram-based Initial Labeling). O método substitui a seleção aleatória ou baseada em incerteza (inexistente no início do processo) pela centralidade filogenética, selecionando amostras representativas que maximizam a diversidade do espaço de características sem a necessidade de um modelo prévio. Por fim, a tese apresenta o framework HERMES (Heterogeneous Ensemble Ranking for Modelfree Early Selection), desenhado para atuar sobre dados heterogêneos na ausência total de oráculos. Utilizando a Fronteira de Pareto para ranquear dados não estruturados, o framework infere classes latentes nos extremos de dominância e propaga rótulos de forma autônoma. Um protocolo de validação de estabilidade, baseado em métricas de Flip-Rate e Taxa de Concordância, foi desenvolvido para calibrar os hiperparâmetros de difusão sem a necessidade de rótulos reais. A aplicação do framework em um estudo de caso real sobre Insegurança Alimentar na cidade de São Paulo demonstrou sua capacidade de traduzir dados socioeconômicos brutos em mapas de vulnerabilidade acionáveis para políticas públicas.

title: Hypernetwork-guided fusion with intra-class MixUp for breast cancer subtyping
abstract: Accurate breast cancer subtyping guides treatment selection, yet histopathology captures morphology without molecular state, while genomic profiling captures molecular signatures without spatial context. Existing fusion methods rely on concatenation, or on attention applied only after each modality is encoded independently. This work identifies a scale-dependent asymmetry in the direction of cross-modal conditioning: the direction that performs best under limited samples is not the one that holds at scale, and the reversal is traced to the capacity of the modulation pathway rather than to the fusion principle. The comparison is carried out within a hypernetwork-guided framework in which an auxiliary network maps one modality to conditioning parameters that modulate the other's feature representation, shaping features at the parametric level rather than the decision stage; modulation is patient-specific rather than patch-specific. Both directions are instantiated-gene-to-image (HyperG2I) and image-to-gene (HyperI2G) - and trained under a label-aware MixUp strategy that interpolates within-class samples across both modalities, preserving the hard binary labels clinical decisions require. The framework is evaluated on two paired TCGA-BRCA cohorts-one limited-sample, one independently assembled at scale-under a single protocol spanning two whole-slide representations, multiple visual backbones, and both conditioning directions. On the limited-sample cohort, gene-to-image conditioning at its optimal augmentation setting exceeds early fusion and both unimodal baselines, giving the highest recall on the aggressive Basal/HER2 class of any configuration evaluated, and an ablation favours intra-class over inter-class mixing. At scale this ordering does not hold: image-to-gene conditioning sustains its performance whereas gene-to-image does not, recovering only partially under the full tissue bag and isolating the capacity of the modulation pathway as the binding constraint. Direction and capacity of cross-modal conditioning, rather than fusion depth alone, therefore govern how such frameworks scale.

title: Deriving Scaling Laws for OpenEuroLLM Models: Learning Rate, Batch Size and Loss
abstract: We study the scaling behavior of learning rate and batch size in pretraining dense large language models on English-prevalent corpora. Beyond scaling jointly optimal learning rates and batch sizes, we investigate their marginal evolution with model capacity and data scale and develop a model that captures these relationships. As we employ a Warmup-Stable-Decay learning rate schedule, we further investigate the gains from learning rate annealing over a broad range of hyperparameters settings, models and data budgets, and whether the optimal learning rate and batch size transfer between the stable and decay phases. Finally, we characterize the dependence of loss on model capacity and dataset size, evaluating recently proposed scaling forms that explicitly model their interaction. We find these approaches particularly effective at capturing both undertraining and overtraining regimes across our experiments. This study establishes a first baseline and scaling procedure for the development of future OpenEuroLLM models. We open-source the complete collection of pretraining runs used in this study.

title: Predicting Turn-Taking Outcomes in Multi-Party Conversation: Interpretable Modelling of Speech and Gaze Dynamics with Interpersonal Closeness
abstract: Smooth speaker transitions are fundamental to effective conversation and rely on an interlocutor's ability to predict when to enter the conversation. This ability depends on accurately interpreting and expressing the verbal and non-verbal cues that signal when a speaker wishes to take or relinquish the floor. The process becomes even more complex in noisy, natural, multi-party settings, with multiple interlocutors available. This study models how gaze and speech, together with perceived interpersonal closeness, signal conversational floor changes in free four-person dialogue. Using the GaMMA corpus, we trained logistic regression models using interpretable, behaviourally motivated features extracted before each turn-taking event to classify floor-transfer outcomes as gaps or overlaps. Predictors included gaze features such as transition motifs and behavioural contrasts, entropy, gaze-based addressee identity, and mutual gaze, alongside speech features derived from speaker loudness, as well as perceived interpersonal closeness (IOS) between speakers. Results show that gaze features capture predictive structure, and that combining them with loudness improves performance (ROC AUC = 0.76 +- 0.04). Loudness reflected speaker control, while gaze dispersion and addressing indexed listener readiness and competitive entry. Performance remained robust across noise conditions, indicating that gaze provides a complementary, noise-resilient cue to turn-taking dynamics.

title: Intelligent Text-Matching System for Compliance Verification of Commercial Vehicles in Active and Passive Safety Research
abstract: The compliance verification of operating vehicles, also known as the verification of compliant vehicles, is a crucial link in ensuring road transportation safety. However, the traditional manual interpretation of the complex remarks in the announcement of compliant vehicle models suffers from low efficiency and is prone to errors. Therefore, this study proposes a multi-level intelligent text matching (MLITM) system framework to automatically determine whether text fragments comply with and explain the differences between the actual vehicles and the parameters in the announcement during the verification process. Methodologically, MLITM adopts a three-level collaborative strategy: rapid filtering through full-text matching; detection of high-similarity segments through the longest common substring matching; and recall of scattered keywords through adaptive sliding window matching. Experiments show that the matching accuracy of MLITM on the simulation dataset is 103.4% higher than that of the regular expression method, with an average processing time of only 26 microseconds and an efficiency improvement of 26 times; among all methods compared in this study, MLITM achieves the best recognition accuracy and recall for various typical samples. Furthermore, by encapsulating the core MLITM algorithm as a microservice module and integrating it into an actual vehicle compliance review system, this study verifies that the proposed method can effectively assist auditors in rapidly locating supporting textual evidence. The results demonstrate its significant potential for improving review efficiency and enhancing the consistency of review outcomes.This system framework provides an efficient and interpretable solution for compliance verification, verifying the feasibility of lightweight AI in vertical fields. Additionally, based on the structured vehicle parameter database generated by this study, it can also provide key data support for active and passive safety research such as the prevention of pedal misoperation in electric commercial vehicles.

title: Research on Automatic Construction Algorithm of Ideological and Political Knowledge Graph in Universities Based on Large Language Model
abstract: Addressing the core pain points in current university ideological and political knowledge graph construction—poor domain adaptability of traditional methods, insufficient entity-relation extraction accuracy, weak implicit knowledge mining capabilities, and the difficulty of general-purpose large models adapting to the rigorous knowledge system and semantic norms of the ideological and political field—this paper proposes a hierarchical entity-relation joint extraction and knowledge calibration algorithm (LLM-HERCKA) driven by a large language model for the ideological and political field. First, a dedicated corpus covering four core ideological and political courses in universities and a fine-tuning paradigm are constructed to achieve deep adaptation of the large model to the ideological and political field. Second, a three-layer ontology architecture for ideological and political knowledge and a hierarchical joint extraction mechanism are designed to solve the error propagation problem of traditional pipeline methods. Finally, a dual-path knowledge calibration module is proposed to ensure the compliance and factual accuracy of extracted knowledge. Experiments were conducted on a self-constructed dataset of 2000 labeled samples for ideological and political education evaluation. Results show that the algorithm achieves an F1 score of 94.27% for entity extraction and 92.58% for relation extraction, representing improvements of 8.35 and 9.76 percentage points respectively compared to the traditional BERT+CRF model, and improvements of 5.12 and 6.34 percentage points respectively compared to the zero-sample extraction of general large-scale models. Ablation experiments validated the effectiveness of each core module. This algorithm can achieve efficient and automated construction of ideological and political knowledge graphs in universities, providing core technical support for digital teaching and intelligent applications of ideological and political education.
